3
Evolutionary Algorithms for Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

3.1 Introduction

The research of evolutionary computation in many areas focuses on the innovation of selection strategies, such as multi‐objective optimization [1], many‐objective optimization [2], and constrained optimization [3]. This is because evolutionary algorithms can generate promising solutions for these problems but are unable to distinguish them to retain the better ones. Thus, novel selection strategies are developed to preserve the population diversity for multi‐objective optimization [4], alleviate the dominance resistance phenomenon for many‐objective optimization [5], and balance between objective optimization and constraint satisfaction for constrained optimization [6]. These selection strategies are combined with the variation operators in genetic algorithms, differential evolution, particle swarm optimization, and other metaheuristics, which are effective enough for obtaining a set of well‐converged and diversified solutions.

However, evolutionary algorithms can hardly generate promising solutions in high‐dimensional decision spaces due to the curse of dimensionality [7]. Even if many metaheuristics and mathematical programming methods have shown fast convergence speed on single‐objective optimization problems, they are inefficient to generate a set of diversified solutions for multi‐objective optimization [8]. Therefore, the research of large‐scale multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) focuses on the innovation of variation operators rather than selection strategies, which should be able to generate high‐quality solutions approximating the Pareto fronts of large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (LSMOPs) with good diversity.

3.1.1 Ideas of Searching in High‐Dimensional Spaces

For large‐scale single‐objective optimization, many metaheuristics have shown outstanding performance on benchmark problems and competitions, such as the advanced variants of differential evolution and particle swarm optimization [9]. Intuitively, the variation operators suggested in these metaheuristics can be equipped with multi‐objective selection strategies for handling LSMOPs. However, the difficulties of single‐objective optimization and multi‐objective optimization are fundamentally different. First, the goal of single‐objective evolutionary algorithms is to approximate the only optimal solution of a problem, which cannot make all solutions in the population well‐converged when solving LSMOPs [10]. Second, it is difficult to distinguish non‐dominated solutions quantitatively, which hinders the parameter adaptation in differential evolution [11, 12] and the learning strategies in particle swarm optimization [13, 14]. As a matter of fact, the popular variation operators for single‐objective optimization and multi‐objective optimization are different. For instance, genetic operators are effective for the diversity preservation in multi‐objective optimization, but they converge slower than many other operators on a single objective [15]. Most variation operators in MOEAs (including those based on differential evolution and particle swarm optimization) are tailed by polynomial mutation for local exploitation [16, 17], while it is rarely used in single‐objective optimization.

First‐order gradient descent methods are particularly effective for the optimization problems with massive variables, such as the training of deep neural networks [18, 19]. Besides, the gradients of black‐box objectives can be well approximated by finite difference [20] and solved by gradient descent methods. However, an inescapable issue is the high computational complexity of gradient calculation, where function evaluations are consumed to calculate the gradients of a solution with decision variables. When solving LSMOPs, gradient descent methods turn out to be less efficient than evolutionary algorithms, since the update of one solution in gradient descent methods takes more function evaluations than the update of a whole population in evolutionary algorithms. This fact seems counterintuitive since all the partial derivatives of some objective functions can be calculated together (e.g., the backpropagation of deep neural networks), which reduces the number of consumed function evaluations from to 1 [21]. Nevertheless, it is assumed that all the partial derivatives cannot be calculated together for generic problems, and the number of consumed function evaluations remains when using finite difference. In addition, gradient descent methods have to aggregate multiple objectives when solving LSMOPs, which can only obtain boundary solutions (i.e., only one objective is minimized) on non‐convex Pareto fronts regardless of the weights for objective aggregation [8].

In short, single‐objective optimizers cannot be directly used for solving LSMOPs. Besides, the convergence speed of evolutionary algorithms cannot be unlimitedly improved due to the curse of dimensionality, which is inevitable in high‐dimensional decision spaces. Considering that LSMOPs are generally NP‐hard problems whose global optimal solutions cannot be found in polynomial time, novel strategies have to be designed to pursue other goals alternatively, such as solving LSMOPs with particular characteristics and finding local optimal solutions.

3.1.2 Taxonomy of Large‐Scale MOEAs

Large‐scale MOEAs can be roughly divided into three categories, including decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs, decision space reduction‐based MOEAs, and novel search strategy‐based MOEAs [22]. As plotted in Fig. 3.1(a), decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs aim to solve LSMOPs in a divide‐and‐conquer manner, where the large number of decision variables is divided into multiple groups and optimized alternately. Assuming that an LSMOP has decision variables with each having candidate values, the total number of candidate solutions can be reduced from to if the decision variables are divided into groups with equal size. That is, the number of candidate solutions is exponentially reduced with the increment of the number of groups . Extremely, each variable is assigned to an independent group making , and thus the number of candidate solutions is minimized to . However, the arbitrary division of decision variables is questionable due to the presence of variable interactions, where the optimal value of a decision variable may depend on the values of other decision variables, and the alternate optimization of these decision variables gets stuck in local optimums.

Taking the following single‐objective optimization problem as an example:

Second, since the minimum value of is when , the global optimum of the problem is when . On the other hand, considering the following single‐objective optimization problem:

where the two decision variables of the problem are also optimized in sequence. First, since the partial derivative decreases with the increment of , the optimal value of can be either 0 or 1. Second, since the minimum value of is 0 when and the minimum value of is 0.1213 when , the global optimum of the problem is 0 when and the local optimum of the problem is 0.1213 when . However, since when , the first step optimizes to 1 with a probability of , which means that the local optimal solution is much more likely to be found than the global optimal solution.

In short, the decision variables in Eq. (3.1) can be separately optimized while the decision variables in Eq. (3.2) cannot. The difference mainly lies in the partial derivatives, where the of Eq. (3.1) is independent of but the of Eq. (3.2) is not. In other words,

(3.3)

holds for Eq. (3.1) and thus the global optimal solution can be found by alternately optimizing and , whereas it does not hold for Eq. (3.2) and thus the global optimal solution cannot be found by alternately optimizing and . The and in Eq. (3.2) are known as interacted decision variables, which can only be divided into the same group and optimized simultaneously. To address this dilemma, a variety of variable grouping methods have been developed for large‐scale optimization, such as random grouping [23], ordered grouping [24], and differential grouping [25]. While these grouping methods were originally tailored for converging to the single optimum of single‐objective optimization problems, they can hardly find multiple solutions spreading over the whole Pareto fronts due to the lack of the consideration of diversity. Therefore, some large‐scale MOEAs divide the decision variables by considering their contributions to convergence and diversity [26–28], where the convergence‐related variables are further divided according to their interactions for converging to the Pareto front, and the diversity‐related variables are simultaneously optimized to enhance the population diversity. Obviously, decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs are only suitable for LSMOPs with separable decision variables. If all the decision variables are interacted with each other like Eq. (3.2), decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs will degenerate into general MOEAs since all the decision variables have to be optimized together.

As plotted in Fig. 3.1(b), decision space reduction‐based MOEAs aim to reduce the number of decision variables of LSMOPs, and thus the total number of candidate solutions can be directly reduced from to , where is the number of reduced decision variables. Considering the following single‐objective optimization problem:

(3.4)

where the global optimum of the problem is when . During the optimization procedure, the desirable setting may be concluded from the non‐dominated solutions in the current population, and thus only needs to be optimized. At each generation, dimensionality reduction methods are used to reduce the number of decision variables of parent solutions according to the current population. Then, offspring solutions are generated by the shortened parent solutions, and they are recovered by dimensionality reduction methods for function evaluation. To reduce the dimensionality of decision spaces, some large‐scale MOEAs develop heuristic methods (e.g., problem transformation [29] and problem reformulation [30]) or adopt machine learning methods (e.g., random embedding [31], principal component analysis [32], neural networks [33], and clustering [34]) to mine the interrelations between decision variables. The dimensionality reduction methods work in an unsupervised manner, which focus on the decision variables of solutions without considering their objective values. Thus, they do not need to consider the interactions between decision variables and are much more efficient than decision variable grouping methods. Nevertheless, the decision variables of many problems like Eqs. (3.1) and (3.2) are unrelated to each other, the elimination of any decision variable is likely to lose the global optimums. Apart from specific LSMOPs such as those with low intrinsic dimensions [31] or sparse optimal solutions [33], decision space reduction‐based MOEAs can quickly converge to the local optimums of LSMOPs, but can hardly approximate the global optimums of LSMOPs even if massive function evaluations are available.

As plotted in Fig. 3.1(c), there exist some large‐scale MOEAs suggesting novel search strategies to directly search in the high‐dimensional decision space. While decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs and decisions space reduction‐based MOEAs employ conventional variation operators (e.g., simulated binary crossover [35], polynomial mutation [36], and differential evolution [37]) to generate offspring solutions after dividing and reducing the dimensionality of decision spaces, respectively, novel search strategy‐based MOEAs aim to enhance the convergence speed by suggesting new methods for offspring generation, including new variation operators and probability models. The new variation operators include particle swarm optimization [38], competitive swarm optimizer [10], memetic evolution [39], and so on [40, 41], and the probability models include the Gaussian process [42], direct sampling [43], covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy [44], generative adversarial networks [45], and so on [46, 47]. In addition, since gradient descent methods converge quickly in high‐dimensional decision spaces, the ideas of gradient‐assisted [8] and pseudo‐gradient‐assisted [48] evolutionary computation are also adopted by MOEAs, where the gradient search is responsible for enhancing the population convergence and the evolutionary search is responsible for retaining the population diversity and escaping from local optimums. As a consequence, novel search strategy‐based MOEAs are very versatile since they make no assumption about the characteristics of LSMOPs and strike a balance between exploitation and exploration in high‐dimensional decision spaces as well as low‐dimensional decision spaces. Novel search strategy‐based MOEAs may not be as efficient as decision variable grouping‐based and decisions space reduction‐based MOEAs, but they are suitable for handling the LSMOPs whose decision variables cannot be divided or decision spaces cannot be reduced.

3.2 Random Grouping‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The cooperative coevolution generalized differential evolution 3 (CCGDE3) is the first MOEA tailored for solving LSMOPs, which is a decision variable grouping‐based MOEA with a random grouping method [23]. Although the random grouping method does not consider the interactions between decision variables, it is very simple and does not introduce additional function evaluations. Moreover, the randomness of the division of decision variables can maintain the interactions to some extent [49], which has inspired many subsequent MOEAs with more advanced grouping methods [50–52].

3.2.1 Random Grouping Method of CCGDE3

Before the optimization procedure, CCGDE3 randomly divides decision variables into groups with equal size and assigns one subpopulation to each variable group to be evolved independently. As described in Algorithm 3.1, the initialization operation begins with the random grouping of all the decision variables (Lines 1–5), where each variable group contains approximately decision variables. Then, a population with solutions is randomly initialized (Line 6), and the decision variables belonging to each group constitute a subpopulation (Line 8). CCGDE3 will evolve the subpopulations separately, where only the decision variables in will be optimized for subpopulation .

It should be noted that a solution with partial decision variables cannot be evaluated on objective functions. Thus, the solutions in each subpopulation should be combined with the solutions in other subpopulations to form complete decision vectors. For this aim, CCGDE3 randomly pairs the solutions as described in Algorithm 3.2. For each solution in subpopulation , a solution is randomly selected from the non‐dominated solutions in all the subpopulations (Line 3), and the decision variables of that do not belong to are set to those of (Line 6). That is, the solutions in subpopulation actually have complete decision vectors, but only the decision variables in mate with each other to generate offspring solutions.

3.2.2 Optimization via GDE3

Except for the coevolution of multiple subpopulations focusing on different decision variables, CCGDE3 does not suggest new variation operators or selection strategies. To evolve each subpopulation, GDE3 [53] is adopted to generate offspring solutions and truncate populations. The environmental selection strategy of GDE3 is an enhancement of that of NSGA‐II, where the crowding distances are iteratively calculated to alleviate the limitation of one‐off selection [4]. As described in Algorithm 3.3, for each offspring solution and its main parent , is used to replace directly if dominates (Line 5). Otherwise, is put into the subpopulation if it is not dominated by (Line 7). After all the offspring solutions are checked, the enlarged population is sorted by non‐dominated sorting (Line 8), and all the solutions in the first non‐dominated fronts are retained, where is the minimum value ensuring that the number of retained solutions is not smaller than the population size (Line 13). To eliminate excessive solutions, the crowding distances of the solutions are calculated (Line 15) and the solution with the smallest crowding distance is eliminated from the th non‐dominated front (Line 16). This operation repeats until the number of retained solutions is equal to (Line 14), and the retained solutions constitute the subpopulation for next generation (Line 17).

3.2.3 Procedure of CCGDE3

With the random grouping method and the optimization procedure of GDE3, the procedure of CCGDE3 is described in Algorithm 3.4. First, the decision variables are divided into groups and subpopulations with solutions are initialized (Line 1). At each generation, each subpopulation is evolved one by one (Line 3), and each solution in the subpopulation is selected as the main parent (Line 5) to generate an offspring solution by using differential evolution and polynomial mutation (Line 7). Note that here only the decision variables corresponding to the subpopulation are changed in the offspring solution. To evaluate the newly generated offspring solutions, they are combined with the solutions in other subpopulations to form complete decision vectors (Line 9). To select solutions from the combination of the subpopulation and its offspring solutions, the environmental selection strategy of GDE3 is adopted (Line 10). Finally, a population is obtained as the output of the algorithm, which consists of solutions selected from all the subpopulations by using the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II (Line 11).

At each generation of CCGDE3, the time complexity is for offspring generation and for environmental selection, where denotes the number of groups, denotes the number of decision variables, and denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of CCGDE3 is .

3.3 Decision Variable Clustering‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The alternate optimization of randomly divided variable groups is likely to get stuck in local optimums, and the population diversity cannot be explicitly maintained among multiple subpopulations. Thus, the large‐scale many‐objective evolutionary algorithm (LMEA) uses two decision variable grouping strategies, namely, differential grouping and decision variable clustering [27], to address the above two issues. At the expense of additional function evaluations, LMEA first divides the decision variables into convergence‐related ones and diversity‐related ones via decision variable clustering, and then divides the convergence‐related variables via differential grouping, thus maintaining population diversity and global optimums. Besides, LMEA updates partial decision variables of a single population at a time, which does not require the random combination of solutions that may generate unpromising decision vectors. The idea of decision variable clustering in LMEA is robust in handling complex relations between decision variables and population convergence/diversity, which has been leveraged by many advanced MOEAs [54–56].

3.3.1 Decision Variable Clustering Method of LMEA

The core contribution of LMEA is the decision variable clustering strategy, which aims to divide all the decision variables into convergence‐related ones and diversity‐related ones to be optimized via different strategies. Convergence‐related variables indicate those mainly affecting the population convergence, i.e., the change of such decision variables changes the distance of a solution to the Pareto front. By contrast, diversity‐related variables indicate those mainly affecting the population diversity, i.e., the change of such decision variables changes the position of a solution on the Pareto front.

Considering the above natures of convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, the decision variable clustering strategy identifies them based on the perturbations of decision variables. As detailed in Algorithm 3.5, given randomly selected solutions for perturbation (Line 2), each decision variable of each solution is randomly perturbed (i.e., assigning a random value within the decision space) for times (Line 4). Thus, there will be solution sets with each having solutions as depicted in Fig. 3.2(a), where denotes the total number of decision variables. Then, a line is fitted for each solution set in the ‐dimensional objective space (Line 5) as depicted in Fig. 3.2(b), where the mean square error of the line is calculated (Line 6) and the angle between the line and is calculated (Line 7), as depicted in Fig. 3.2(c). Obviously, a smaller angle indicates that the solutions generated by perturbing a decision variable have greater difference in terms of distances to the Pareto front, and thus the decision variable is more likely to be a convergence‐related variable. By contrast, a larger angle indicates that the solutions generated by perturbing a decision variable have greater difference in terms of positions on the Pareto front, and thus the decision variable is more likely to be a diversity‐related variable.

Therefore, to distinguish between convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, the angles of the lines generated by the perturbations on each decision variable can be used as features for clustering. As depicted in Fig. 3.2(d), ‐means is used to divide the decision variables into two groups according to the angles of lines (Line 8), where the group with decision variables corresponding to smaller angles are identified as convergence‐related variables, and the group with decision variables corresponding to larger angles are identified as diversity‐related variables (Lines 9–11).

3.3.2 Interaction Analysis of LMEA

While the population diversity can be enhanced by fine‐tuning diversity‐related variables, the population convergence has to be ensured by fully optimizing convergence‐related variables. That is, the optimal values of convergence‐related variables are likely to be unique but the optimal values of diversity‐related variables are not. Thus, LMEA further divides convergence‐related variables into multiple groups to optimize them in a divide‐and‐conquer manner, where the convergence‐related variables in different groups are not interacted with any others to ensure that the global optimums are not lost. For this aim, a differential grouping method [25] is adopted to detect variable interactions based on perturbations. More specifically, decision variable is interacted with decision variable if there exist a solution and four variable values such that

In practice, the solution is randomly selected from the population, the variable values are the original ones of , and the variable values are randomly sampled. Therefore, three additional function evaluations are needed to calculate the objective values of , , and . Moreover, in terms of multi‐objective optimization, is interacted with if the above conditions hold on any objective .

In order to maintain the global optimums, all the interacted convergence‐related variables should be assigned to the same group. For example, if is interacted with , is interacted with , but is not interacted with , then the three variables should be assigned to the same group. Thus, the detection between and is unnecessary if has been verified to have interacted with and has been verified to have interacted with , and many unnecessary function evaluations can be saved. As detailed in Algorithm 3.6, LMEA checks the interactions between each convergence‐related variable and those in existing groups (Line 9), on the basis of solutions randomly selected from the population (Line 8). Then, if is not interacted with any variable in existing groups, it is assigned to a new group (Line 16). While if is interacted with some variables in multiple groups, all these groups together with constitute a new group (Lines 18–20). In this case, LMEA need not to detect the interactions between all pairs of convergence‐related variables, thus saving many function evaluations especially when many variables are interacted with each other.

3.3.3 Convergence Optimization and Diversity Optimization

After performing decision variable clustering and interaction analysis, some groups of convergence‐related variables and one group of diversity‐related variables are obtained. To fully optimize convergence‐related variables for good convergence and fine‐tune diversity‐related variables for good diversity, LMEA suggests two different optimization procedures carried out on convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, respectively. The optimization of convergence‐related variables is elaborated in Algorithm 3.7, which begins with the non‐dominated sorting on the current population (Line 1) and the calculation of the distances between solutions in the current population to the origin in the objective space (Line 2). Thus, both the non‐dominated front number and the distance to the origin can measure the convergence degree of a solution, and the convergence‐related variables of a solution with better convergence degree are more likely to be optimized. For each group of convergence‐related variables, LMEA generates new offspring solutions by changing only the variables in the group (Line 5), where is the population size. Based on the non‐dominated front numbers, some solutions are selected from the current population and put into the mating pool (Line 9), and offspring solutions are generated by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 14) based on two solutions selected via binary tournament selection (Line 12). Then, each offspring solution is associated with a parent in , where all the decision variables outside the current group of are set to the same as those of (Line 13). This way, only the decision variables in the current group are changed. After the generation of offspring solutions, each of them is used to replace its parent in the population if it has a smaller non‐dominated front number or distance to the origin (Line 20). Since LMEA focuses on improving the population convergence without considering the population diversity, the selection strategies consider the convergence degrees rather than the diversity degrees of solutions. In fact, since diversity‐related variables keep unchanged during the optimization procedure, the population diversity is also unchanged in most cases.

The optimization of diversity‐related variables is elaborated in Algorithm 3.8, which is similar to general MOEAs as both the population convergence and population diversity are taken into consideration. By generating offspring solutions by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 5) based on two solutions randomly selected from the current population, each offspring solution is associated with a unique parent in the population. That is, all the convergence‐related variables of are set to the same as those of (Line 4); in other words, only the diversity‐related variables are changed. After the generation of offspring solutions, they are combined with the current population and solutions are selected and survive to the next generation. Here, LMEA selects solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers (Line 13) and selects solutions from the last non‐dominated front one by one according to their angles to the solutions having been selected (Line 16). This selection strategy adopts the non‐dominated sorting of NSGA‐II [57] and the truncation strategy of SPEA2 [58], which inherits the merits of both the two MOEAs for retaining solutions with good convergence and diversity.

3.3.4 Procedure of LMEA

With the decision variable clustering, interaction analysis, convergence optimization, and diversity optimization, the procedure of LMEA is described in Algorithm 3.9. First, a population with solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), which is then used to divide all the decision variables into convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables (Line 2), and divide the convergence‐related variables into some groups (Line 3). At each generation, the convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables are alternately optimized (Lines 5 and 6), where only a single population is evolved during the whole optimization procedure. Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 7).

At each generation of LMEA, the time complexity is for both convergence optimization and diversity optimization, where denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of LMEA is .

3.4 Problem Reformulation‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

Different from decision variable grouping, the large‐scale multi‐objective framework (LSMOF) aims to directly reduce the dimensionality of decision spaces, so as to solve a small‐scale optimization problem rather than a large‐scale one. Instead of optimizing all the decision variables of an LSMOP, LSMOF optimizes two weight variables for each of solutions, where the combination of a weight variable and a solution leads to a new solution for approximating the Pareto set. Thus, the dimensionality of the decision space is reduced from to . By maximizing the HV [59] value of the new solutions, LSMOF reformulates the LSMOP into a small‐scale single‐objective optimization problem. LSMOF can quickly converge to local optimums due to the dimensionality reduction of decision spaces, but can hardly approximate the global optimums due to the inexistence of the global optimums in the reduced decision spaces. Owing to the rapid convergence speed of LSMOF, the idea of problem reformulation has been carried forward in many other MOEAs for solving LSMOPs [60–62].

3.4.1 Problem Reformulation of LSMOF

The problem reformulation method of LSMOF converts an LSMOP into a small‐scale single‐objective optimization problem to be solved by differential evolution. For the reformulated problem, the decision variables are a number of weight variables generating new solutions based on the existing ones, and the objective is the HV value of all the new solutions. As described in Algorithm 3.10, the nadir point (i.e., a point containing the maximum values of all the objectives) of the current population is first obtained as the reference point for HV calculation (Line 1). Then, reference solutions are selected from via an environmental selection strategy (Line 2). It is worth noting that LSMOF is a framework compatible with many existing MOEAs, where NSGA‐II with non‐dominated sorting and crowding distance‐based selection strategy is adopted here. For each reference solution , two weight variables and are introduced to generate two new solutions and , that is,

As illustrated in Fig. 3.3, locates on the line through and , where the distance between and is determined by the weight variable . Similarly, locates on the line through and , where the distance between and is determined by the weight variable . Thus, the intersections of the two lines and the Pareto set are Pareto optimal solutions, which can be found by finding the optimal values of and . That is, the optimization of the decision variables of an LSMOP is converted into the optimization of two weight variables.

Since the optimization of the weight variables of a reference solution cannot explicitly specify the location of the new solution on the Pareto front, LSMOF optimizes the weight variables of reference solutions together to enhance both the population convergence and population diversity (Line 6). To evaluate the new solutions generated by weight variable optimization, LSMOF calculates the HV value of all the new solutions (Line 7), where a higher HV value indicates a better convergence and diversity of the new solutions. As a consequence, LSMOF reformulates an LSMOP into the following single‐objective optimization problem:

This way, the number of variables to be optimized is decreased from to , and the dimensionality of the decision space is considerably reduced. The problem reformulation significantly increases the convergence speed on LSMOPs, but it can hardly approximate the global optimums since the one‐dimensional lines may not intersect the ‐dimensional Pareto set in the ‐dimensional decision space, where the number of objectives is much smaller than the number of decision variables .

3.4.2 Single‐Objective Optimization of LSMOF

To fully optimize the weight variables of best solutions in the current population, LSMOF adopts differential evolution to maximize the reformulated problem , where the detailed procedure is presented in Algorithm 3.11. More specifically, solutions are first generated as the initial population (Line 1), where each solution is a vector of . Then, the initial population is evaluated on (Line 5) and optimized for generations (Line 6). Note that here the evaluation of a solution consumes function evaluations on the original LSMOP. To update each solution at each generation, a new solution is generated by differential evolution based on three solutions randomly selected from the current population (Lines 8 and 9), and is used to replace in the population if the former has a better objective value on (Lines 12 and 13). During the optimization procedure, LSMOF saves all the newly generated solutions for the original LSMOP in an archive (Lines 4 and 10), which is the output of the single‐objective optimization procedure (Line 14). The solutions in the archive will be combined with the current population, and then truncated by an environmental selection strategy for the next round of optimization.

3.4.3 Procedure of LSMOF

With the problem reformulation and single‐objective optimization, the procedure of LSMOF is described in Algorithm 3.12, which begins with the random initialization of a population with solutions (Line 1). At each generation, if the ratio of consumed function evaluations is less than a predefined threshold , LSMOF reformulates the LSMOP (Line 4) and optimizes the weight variables via single‐objective differential evolution algorithm (Line 5), where the solutions generated during the single‐objective optimization procedure are combined with the population and truncated by non‐dominated sorting and crowding distance‐based selection (Line 6). Otherwise, LSMOF optimizes the population by using the mating selection strategy, genetic operators, and environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II until termination (Lines 8–10). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of LSMOF, the time complexity is for problem reformulation and for single‐objective optimization, where denotes the number of objectives, denotes the number of reference solutions, denotes the population size for single‐objective optimization, and denotes the number of generations for single‐objective optimization. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of LSMOF is .

3.5 Competitive Swarm Optimizer‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

In addition to dividing the decision variables or reducing the number of decision variables, the large‐scale multi‐objective competitive swarm optimizer (LMOCSO) suggests a new variation operator for optimizing all the decision variables of LSMOPs together. With no assumption of the relations between decision variables, LMOCSO searches in the original decision spaces and follows a similar optimization procedure as general MOEAs. Although LMOCSO is less effective than decision variable group‐based and decision space reduction‐based MOEAs on particular LSMOPs, it is flexible to handle complex LSMOPs with a robust performance and has also been used in subsequent algorithms [63, 64].

3.5.1 Enhanced Competitive Swarm Optimizer of LMOCSO

In comparison to genetic algorithms that are widely adopted in MOEAs, particle swarm optimization converges faster in high‐dimensional decision spaces due to the learning strategies between particles. However, particle swarm optimization is not popular for multi‐objective optimization due to the difficulty in selecting best particles and maintaining the population diversity. By contrast, competitive swarm optimizer (CSO) is more flexible, which generates solutions in a similar way as genetic operators and is compatible with the selection strategies of many existing MOEAs. 3.6 Experimental Comparisons

To investigate the performance of CCGDE3, LMEA, LSMOF, and LMOCSO, they are compared with two representative MOEAs on benchmark LSMOPs. The compared MOEAs include NSGA‐II [57] and GDE3 [53], which are based on genetic algorithms and differential evolution, respectively. The tested benchmark LSMOPs include DTLZ1–DTLZ4 [67] and LSMOP1–LSMOP4 [68], where the number of objectives is set to 2 and the number of decision variables is set to 100, 200, and 500. The population size is set to 100 and the number of function evaluations is set to ; besides, the number of function evaluations for LSMOF is set to 100,000. The populations obtained by the compared algorithms are assessed by IGD [69].

Table 3.1 presents the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold and the statistically similar ones are highlighted. It can be found that the three algorithms LMEA, LSMOF, and LMOCSO exhibit the best overall performance and obtain the best results on all the test instances, which verify the effectiveness of their search strategies (i.e., decision variable grouping, decision space reduction, and novel variation operator) for solving LSMOPs. By contrast, CCGDE3 is not effective due to the simple random grouping strategy. For the problems DTLZ1–DTLZ4 without variable interaction, LMEA and LSMOF obtain the best performance by using the decision variable clustering‐based divide‐and‐conquer search and the problem reformulation‐based decision space reduction method, respectively. For the problems LSMOP1–LSMOP4 with complex variable interactions, LMOCSO obtains the best performance by using an enhanced CSO operator.

Moreover, Fig. 3.5 depicts the convergence profiles of IGD values obtained by the compared MOEAs on DTLZ1 and LSMOP1 with 100 decision variables. For CCGDE3, it converges more slowly than the other MOEAs, which indicates the ineffectiveness of the random grouping method for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. For LMEA, it converges slowly at the beginning since many function evaluations are consumed for the sake of decision variable clustering, but it can obtain promising populations at last by using the divide‐and‐conquer search. For LSMOF, it converges much more quickly than the other MOEAs, but it is likely to get stuck in local optimums, especially on LSMOP1 with complex variable interactions. As for LMOCSO, it converges fast on LSMOP1 with complex variable interactions, but it gets stuck in local optimums on DTLZ1 due to the ineffectiveness of particle swarm optimization in handling multimodal landscapes.

3.7 Summary

This chapter introduces four representative MOEAs for solving LSMOPs. The most significant feature of these MOEAs is that they suggest different ideas to handle the high‐dimensional decision spaces, such as the decision variable grouping methods in CCGDE3 and LMEA, the decision space reduction method in LSMOF, and the novel variation operator in LMOCSO. According to the discussions and experimental results, different types of large‐scale MOEAs are effective for different types of LSMOPs, while no MOEA can obtain the best performance on all types of LSMOPs. For example, decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs are good at solving LSMOPs with few variable interactions, decision space reduction‐based MOEAs can quickly converge to local optimums of LSMOPs with simple Pareto sets, and novel search strategy‐based MOEAs are more robust in solving complex LSMOPs. Besides, most large‐scale MOEAs are ineffective for solving small‐scale problems. After all, if large‐scale MOEAs dominate general MOEAs on small‐scale problems, the latter will become meaningless and the research of large‐scale multi‐objective optimization will not be separated from the research of multi‐objective optimization.

4
Evolutionary Algorithms for Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

4.1 Introduction

The “curse of dimensionality” encountered by evolutionary algorithms in huge decision spaces is inevitable, as they iteratively search for better solutions in a black‐box manner. In addition to developing multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) for solving general LSMOPs, it is reasonable to improve the convergence speed by involving problem‐specific information in offspring generation, such as the gradients used in mathematical programming methods [1]. While it is costly to customize an evolutionary algorithm for every single LSMOP through human expertise, developing effective search strategies for specific types of LSMOPs turns out to be desirable.

4.1.1 Characteristics of Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization Problems

In real‐world applications, there exist many optimization problems having sparse optimal solutions, in which the optimal values of most decision variables are zero. For the neural network training task in supervised learning [2], the goal is to find the optimal weights between layers, where many weights are expected to be zero for alleviating overfitting. Hence, the optimal solutions for neural network training are sparse when real encoding is used, where each decision variable denotes a weight. For the frequent pattern mining task in data mining [3], the goal is to find the most frequent and complete pattern (e.g., a set of items) from a transaction dataset (e.g., a set of historical shopping lists having many candidate items), where only a small proportion of all the candidate items is preferred. Hence, the optimal solutions for frequent pattern mining are sparse when binary encoding is used, where each decision variable denotes whether an item is selected or not.

The above tasks are collectively known as sparse optimization problems, which are likely to contain a large number of decision variables. For the aforementioned examples, a neural network should have enough weights for learning complex mappings between features and labels [4], and a transaction dataset usually consists of abundant candidate items for recommending the most complete patterns to customers [5]. Furthermore, sparse optimization problems generally have multiple conflicting objectives to be optimized. For some sparse LSMOPs like neural network training, the sparsity of optimal solutions is explicitly defined as an objective to be optimized (e.g., the network complexity). While for some other sparse LSMOPs like the frequent pattern mining, the sparsity of optimal solutions is implicitly determined by all the objectives (e.g., in Eq. (2.28), the selected items should occupy a small proportion of all the items in a transaction dataset , otherwise will be empty).

4.1.2 Ideas of Finding Sparse Solutions

It is possible to solve sparse LSMOPs using general large‐scale MOEAs, but their efficiency cannot meet the requirement in real‐world scenarios due to the relatively expensive objective functions. For example, evaluating a solution for neural network training needs to calculate the output of all the training samples, and evaluating a solution for frequent pattern mining should traverse the whole transaction dataset. Fortunately, the sparse nature of the optimal solutions of sparse LSMOPs is known in advance, making it possible to optimize only the nonzero variables. Since the nonzero variables are much fewer than the zero variables of sparse LSMOPs, the problems can be considerably eased and many function evaluations can be saved. In comparison to optimizing all the decision variables of general LSMOPs, there are two tasks in solving sparse LSMOPs, including finding the nonzero variables and optimizing the nonzero variables. Furthermore, for the sparse LSMOPs with binary encoding (e.g., frequent pattern mining), the task of optimizing the nonzero variables can be omitted.

Since large‐scale MOEAs focus on continuous optimization, they are suitable for optimizing the nonzero variables but unsuitable for finding the nonzero variables of sparse LSMOPs, where the latter is essentially a binary optimization problem. On the other hand, binary‐coded MOEAs (e.g., NSGA‐II with uniform crossover and bitwise mutation [6]) are also inefficient for finding nonzero variables since they are not tailored for finding sparse solutions. Taking the random initialization strategy as an example, the expectation of the number of zero variables equals the expectation of the number of nonzero variables in the initial solutions. However, since in the optimal solutions of sparse LSMOPs, the initial solutions are far away from the optimal solutions and many function evaluations should be consumed for the sake of convergence. Similarly, for the bitwise mutation flipping each decision variable with the same probability, assuming that a solution having nonzero variables and zero variables is mutated with a probability of on each dimension, the expectation of the number of nonzero variables after one mutation will be

To address the difficulties encountered by large‐scale MOEAs and binary‐coded MOEAs in finding the nonzero variables of sparse LSMOPs, several sparse MOEAs have been proposed in recent years, each of which develops novel strategies to find nonzero variables and adopts existing operators to optimize nonzero variables. In the following sections, three representative sparse MOEAs are introduced and empirically compared.

4.2 Bi‐Level Encoding‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The sparse evolutionary algorithm (SparseEA) is the first generic evolutionary algorithm for solving sparse LSMOPs [7]. The main contribution of SparseEA is to represent each solution by using a bi‐level encoding, which differentiates the search of nonzero variables and the optimization of nonzero variables. Moreover, a population initialization strategy, a crossover operator, and a mutation operator are customized to address the shortcomings of those in binary‐coded MOEAs, thus facilitating the search of nonzero variables.

4.2.1 Bi‐Level Encoding of SparseEA

Formally, SparseEA represents a solution with a binary vector and a real vector , where the decision variables are calculated as

(4.4)

That is, SparseEA stores and instead of during the optimization. For instance, a binary vector and a real vector correspond to a solution . In this way, the optimization of the binary vector is responsible for the search of nonzero variables, and the optimization of the real vector is responsible for the optimization of nonzero variables. It is worth noting that although the introduction of binary vector doubles the number of variables to be optimized, all the form a binary search space that is much smaller than the continuous decision space, and all the real variables corresponding to need not be optimized anymore. In other words, the search space is highly reduced by optimizing many variables in to zero. Besides, the bi‐level encoding parallelizes the search and optimization of nonzero variables, which achieves high efficiency in searching for sparse optimal solutions.

As a matter of fact, the effectiveness of such a bi‐level encoding has been verified on specific applications such as neural network training [8] and portfolio optimization [9], while SparseEA adopts it as a generic strategy for solving various sparse LSMOPs. In SparseEA, the optimization of real vectors is implemented by general strategies used in real‐coded MOEAs, while the optimization of binary vectors is implemented by customized strategies for ensuring the sparsity of generated solutions. These customized strategies include a population initialization strategy, a crossover operator, and a mutation operator.

4.2.2 Population Initialization Strategy of SparseEA

In comparison to random initialization where the sparsity (i.e., the ratio of nonzero variables) of the generated solutions is approximately 0.5, the population initialization strategy of SparseEA aims to generate a set of solutions with different sparsity, thereby better approximating the optimal solutions whose sparsity is unknown. Moreover, SparseEA estimates the probability that each dimension of the binary vector should be zero, which can benefit the search of nonzero variables.

The pseudocode of the population initialization strategy of SparseEA is presented in Algorithm 4.1. To begin with, a solution set with solutions is generated for calculating the scores (Line 1). For the binary vector of the th solution in , all of its binary variables are set to zero (Line 3), except for the th binary variable being one (Line 4). For the real vector of the th solution in , it is randomly sampled in the decision space for continuous sparse LSMOPs (Line 6) and set to a vector of ones for binary sparse LSMOPs (Line 8). That is, the real variables of all the solutions are fixed to one when solving binary sparse LSMOPs, while only the binary variables need to be optimized. Then, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1, the quality of all the solutions in are measured by non‐dominated sorting, where the non‐dominated front numbers of all the solutions constitute a vector (Line 10). Obviously, a smaller non‐dominated front number indicates a better quality of the solution whose th decision variable is nonzero, which implies a lower probability that the th dimension of the binary vector should be zero. Therefore, it is reasonable to use the vector to guide the generation of the binary vectors of solutions, where a binary variable with a lower value is more likely to be set to one, and vice versa. In the population initialization, crossover operator, and mutation operator of SparseEA, the binary variables to be flipped are selected by binary tournament selection according to the vector .

Afterward, a population with solutions is initialized by generating the solutions one by one (Line 12). The generation of a new solution begins with setting its binary vector to a vector of zeros (Line 13). Then, two dimensions are randomly selected (Line 15) and the one corresponding to a lower value is flipped to one (Lines 16–19). This operation repeats for times to diversify the sparsity of the generated solutions (Line 14), where denotes a uniformly distributed random number within . As for the real vector of the new solution, it is randomly sampled in the decision space for continuous sparse LSMOPs (Line 21) and set to a vector of ones for binary sparse LSMOPs (Line 23). Lastly, both the initial population and the vector are returned (Line 25).

4.2.3 Crossover and Mutation Operators of SparseEA

In SparseEA, the real vectors of offspring solutions are generated through simulated binary crossover [10] and polynomial mutation [11], which are the same as most multi‐objective genetic algorithms. On the contrary, the binary vectors of offspring solutions are generated through new crossover and mutation operators, which are designed on the basis of uniform crossover and bitwise mutation, respectively. Similar to the population initialization strategy of SparseEA, the vector is additionally involved in the new crossover and mutation operators to ensure the sparsity of offspring. The pseudocode of the crossover and mutation operators of SparseEA is presented in Algorithm 4.2, where the binary vectors of two parents are used to generate the binary vector of one offspring solution each time, and the real vectors of the same parents are used to generate the real vector of the same offspring solution (Line 3).

First, the binary vector of the offspring solution is set to the same as the first parent (Line 5), and one of the following two operations is performed with the same probability: randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in (Line 7), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a higher value to zero (Lines 8–11); or randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in (Line 13), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a lower value to one (Lines 14–17). In short, the new crossover operator flips a zero variable or a nonzero variable with the same probability, hence, the and of each solution keep unchanged, and the sparsity of offspring solutions can be ensured.

Second, the binary vector of the offspring solution is then mutated by one of the following two operations with the same probability: randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in (Line 19), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a higher value to zero (Lines 20–23); or randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in (Line 25), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a lower value to one (Lines 26–29). Obviously, the new mutation operator can also ensure the sparsity since it flips a zero variable or a nonzero variable of each offspring solution with the same probability.

Third, when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs, the real vector of the offspring solution is generated by performing simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation on and (Line 31). When solving binary sparse LSMOPs, the real vector is always set to a vector of ones without performing crossover or mutation (Line 33). Lastly, the offspring population is returned (Line 35).

4.2.4 Procedure of SparseEA

With the new population initialization strategy, crossover operator, and mutation operator for generating sparse solutions, the procedure of SparseEA is detailed in Algorithm 4.3. First of all, a population with solutions is initialized and the vector is calculated by the new population initialization strategy (Line 1). Then, the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of each solution in are determined (Lines 2 and 3). At each generation, the mating pool is constructed by selecting parents from the population via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances of solutions (Line 5). After that, offspring solutions are generated by the new crossover and mutation operators (Line 6). To select solutions from the combination of and , SparseEA adopts the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II [6] for simplicity, where solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 7). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 8).

It can be concluded from Algorithm 4.1 that the calculation of is relatively time‐consuming for large‐scale optimization due to the use of non‐dominated sorting, which holds a time complexity of for solving a problem with objectives and decision variables [12]. Nevertheless, this operation is not in the main loop of the algorithm. At each generation of SparseEA, the time complexity is for mating pool selection, for offspring generation, and for environmental selection. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of SparseEA is , which is the same as many other MOEAs.

4.3 Machine Learning‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm

The multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm based on Pareto optimal subspace learning (MOEA/PSL) inherits the bi‐level encoding of SparseEA, where unsupervised neural networks are adopted to learn the Pareto optimal subspace according to the current population [13]. More specifically, a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) is used to learn a sparse distribution from the binary vectors, and a denoising auto‐encoder (DAE) is used to learn a compact representation from the real vectors. By generating offspring solutions in the Pareto optimal subspace rather than in the original decision space, the search space is highly reduced and the optimization of the binary vectors and real vectors can be considerably eased.

Auto‐encoder serves as the building block of stacked auto‐encoder, which is a three‐layer neural network for the dimensionality of inputs with real encoding [16]. In fact, the output layer of auto‐encoder is the same as the input layer, and thus the propagation from the hidden layer to the output layer is similar to the reconstruction operation of RBM. Assuming that the weights between the input layer and hidden layer are stored in a matrix and the weights between the hidden layer and output layer are stored in a matrix , the hidden layer can be calculated based on an input vector :

Given a set of training samples as input vectors, an auto‐encoder can be trained by using gradient descent [17] for minimizing the difference between each pair of and in an unsupervised manner. Thus, the hidden layer can be used as a reduced representation of for . In MOEA/PSL, the DAE rather than the original auto‐encoder is used, which is a popular variant that randomly sets the elements in each input vector to zero [18].

4.3.2 Pareto Optimal Subspace Learning in MOEA/PSL

As illustrated in Fig. 4.2, since RBM can learn the probability distribution of the input obeying a binomial distribution, it is desirable to learn a sparse distribution from the binary vectors used in bi‐level encoding. Analogously, since DAE can learn a compact representation of the input in a continuous space, it is desirable to reduce the dimensionality of the real vectors used in bi‐level encoding. By using the promising solutions found so far as training samples, the reduced binary vectors and real vectors form a promising approximation of the Pareto optimal subspace. Therefore, the efficiency of finding sparse optimal solutions can be improved by evolving a population in the learnt subspace, even if the search strategies in general MOEAs are employed.

In comparison to other dimensionality reduction methods such as principal component analysis, the advantages of RBM and DAE lie in the fact that they can learn nonlinear interactions between real variables and interactions between binary variables. More importantly, the reduced binary vectors and real vectors can be easily recovered as shown in Fig. 4.2, which is necessary for the function evaluation of decision vectors.

The pseudocode of the Pareto optimal subspace learning‐based offspring generation is presented in Algorithm 4.4. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are used to train an RBM (Lines 1 and 2), and the real vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are used to train a DAE (Lines 4 and 5). Note that the training of DAE can be omitted when solving binary sparse LSMOPs. Afterwards, the binary vectors of two parents are used to generate the binary vectors of two offspring solutions each time, and the real vectors of the same parents are used to generate the real vectors of the same offspring solutions (Line 8). The generation of binary vectors is implemented by uniform crossover and bitwise mutation, and the generation of real vectors is implemented by simulated binary crossover [10] and polynomial mutation [11]. Besides, the probability of generating offspring in the learnt subspace is controlled by a parameter .

When generating two offspring solutions, if , the two binary vectors are first reduced to two binary vectors via RBM (Line 11), then two binary vectors are generated by uniform crossover and bitwise mutation (Line 12), and they are further recovered via RBM to obtain two binary vectors (Line 13). Also, when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs, the two real vectors are first reduced to two real vectors via DAE (Line 15), then two real vectors are generated by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 16), and they are further recovered via DAE to obtain two real vectors (Line 17). When solving binary sparse LSMOPs, the real vectors of offspring solutions are directly set to vectors of ones (Line 19). By contrast, if , the binary vectors are directly used to generate (Line 21), and the real vectors are directly used to generate (Line 23) when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs.

4.3.3 Parameter Adaptation in MOEA/PSL

As can be observed from the above procedure, the probability of generating offspring in the learnt subspace and the hidden layer size of the neural networks are given in advance. Intuitively, a larger generates more offspring solutions in the learnt subspace, but also leads to poorer population diversity. A smaller learns a smaller subspace for higher convergence speed, but also increases the possibility of trapping into local optimums. In order to strike a good balance between greed and randomness, the two parameters should be carefully set. Instead of predefining the parameters by users, MOEA/PSL suggests a parameter adaptation strategy to dynamically estimate the values of and according to the current population.

The pseudocode of the parameter adaptation in MOEA/PSL is described in Algorithm 4.5. At the end of each generation, the number of offspring solutions generated in the learnt subspace that successfully survives to the next generation and the number of offspring solutions generated in the original decision space that successfully survives to the next generation are determined (Lines 1 and 2), and the parameter is updated (Line 3):

Obviously, a larger indicates higher performance of generating offspring in the learnt subspace, hence is increased to generate more offspring solutions in the learnt subspace at the next generation. By contrast, a larger indicates higher performance of generating offspring in the original decision space, hence is decreased to generate more offspring solutions in the original decision space at the next generation. Then, the non‐dominated solution set in the current population is identified (Line 4), and the probability that the decision vector being one can be estimated based on (Line 5):

(4.12)

where if and 1 otherwise. Afterwards, the value of each element can be sampled by comparing with a uniformly distributed random number within :

(4.13)

and the parameter can be calculated (Line 6):

(4.14)

This way, approximates the number of nonzero variables in the decision vector, which is reasonable to be used as the hidden layer size to eliminate the zero variables from the Pareto optimal subspace.

4.3.4 Procedure of MOEA/PSL

With the Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy and parameter adaptation strategy, the procedure of MOEA/PSL is described in Algorithm 4.6. Firstly, a population with solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), and the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of each solution in are determined (Lines 2 and 3). Then, the parameters and are initialized (Lines 4 and 5). At each generation, the mating pool is constructed by selecting parents from the population via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances of solutions (Line 7). After that, offspring solutions are generated by the unsupervised neural network‐based Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy (Line 8). To select solutions from the combination of and , MOEA/PSL adopts the same environmental selection strategy as SparseEA, where solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 9). Furthermore, the parameters and are updated by the parameter adaptation strategy (Line 10). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of MOEA/PSL, the time complexity is for neural network training, for offspring generation, for environmental selection, and for parameter adaptation, where denotes the number of epochs for training, denotes the number of decision variables, and denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of MOEA/PSL is .

4.4 Data Mining‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm

The pattern mining‐based multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (PM‐MOEA) also focuses on the dimensionality reduction of the decision spaces of sparse LSMOPs [19]. In contrast to MOEA/PSL using unsupervised neural networks, PM‐MOEA suggests a novel evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to mine the sparse distribution from the binary vectors, which is quite different and more flexible than machine learning methods. Furthermore, PM‐MOEA suggests a binary crossover operator and a binary mutation operator for ensuring the sparsity of offspring solutions. In comparison to the binary operators of SparseEA flipping a single variable, the expectation of the number of flipped variables is controllable in PM‐MOEA and thus is more flexible to be used.

4.4.1 Evolutionary Frequent Pattern Mining

As introduced in Section 4.1.1, frequent pattern mining aims to find the optimal patterns from a transaction dataset [3]. In addition to considering it as a sparse LSMOP, it is also an effective tool for dimensionality reduction. In particular for solving sparse LSMOPs, the current population can be regarded as a transaction dataset with each decision vector being a transaction, and the set of nonzero variables is the optimal pattern to be mined. This way, the set of nonzero variables can be estimated through frequent pattern mining techniques to guide the offspring generation in later generations, and the dimensionality of the binary search space is naturally reduced.

According to Eq. (2.28), the optimal patterns are the most frequent and complete item sets of the transaction dataset. For solving sparse LSMOPs, the optimal patterns are the minimum estimations of the nonzero variable set, in which each binary variable is probably set to one. In addition, PM‐MOEA also aims to obtain the maximum estimations of the nonzero variable set, in which each binary variable is possibly set to one. More specifically, when generating offspring solutions, the binary variables out of the maximum estimation are always set to zero, the binary variables in the maximum estimation are determined by parents, and the binary variables in the minimum estimation are always set to one. For this aim, PM‐MOEA suggests two objectives for mining the maximum estimations:

(4.15)

and two objectives for mining the minimum estimations:

(4.16)

where is an estimation of the nonzero variable set, is the set of binary vectors of all the non‐dominated solutions in the current population, denotes the set of binary vectors whose nonzero variables form a subset of the nonzero variables in , and denotes the set of binary vectors whose nonzero variables form a superset of the nonzero variables in . Table 4.1 presents an example to illustrate the calculation of the four objectives.

It can be found that the objectives and are the same as and in Eq. (2.28), where aims to find a minimum candidate set being an intersection set of the nonzero variables in all the binary vectors, and makes the minimum candidate set as large as possible. On the other hand, the objectives are are novel, where aims to find a maximum candidate set being a union set of the nonzero variables in all the binary vectors, and makes the maximum candidate set as small as possible. At the beginning of the optimization procedure, the maximum candidate set is likely to contain most variables and the minimum candidate set is likely to contain few variables. With the evolution of the population, the maximum candidate set will be shortened and the minimum candidate set will be enlarged, and the nonzero variable set can be exactly found when the maximum candidate set equals the minimum candidate set. In comparison to machine learning‐based dimensionality reduction methods, frequent pattern mining has three main advantages: first, it mines the maximum and minimum candidate sets of nonzero variables rather than an exact estimation of nonzero variables, where the former are less greedy and can better tackle the inaccuracy of the binary vectors in the current population (since the current population is not optimal). Second, it provides multiple maximum candidate sets and minimum candidate sets, which can make diverse trade‐offs between and or and , thus preserving the population diversity in the decision space. Third, it does not contain any hyperparameter that needs to be tuned (e.g., the hidden layer size of RBM and DAE), which is flexible to be used since the ratio of nonzero variables in the optimal solutions is unknown.

It is obvious that the mining of maximum candidate sets and the mining of minimum candidate sets are also sparse LSMOPs, which have the same number of binary variables as the original sparse LSMOP. Nevertheless, the former are computationally cheap since they are pursued based on the binary vectors of the current population, regardless of the objectives or dataset of the original sparse LSMOP. While many practical frequent pattern mining methods have been proposed [3, 5, 20], they are inefficient for finding diverse patterns. Thus, PM‐MOEA suggests a fast evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to mine the maximum and minimum candidate sets of nonzero variables, which is actually the same as PM‐MOEA itself. Although the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method is adopted twice at each generation, it does not consume many computational resources since it uses a few function evaluations to evolve the population in an incremental manner, i.e., the final population in the previous mining operation is used as the initial population in the next mining operation.

4.4.2 Mining Candidate Sets in PM‐MOEA

As illustrated in Fig. 4.3, the whole binary vector is divided into four parts. First, the variables being zero in all the binary vectors are directly fixed to zero and ignored in the mining operation. After obtaining the maximum and minimum candidate sets, the variables out of the maximum candidate set are also fixed to zero, the variables in the maximum candidate set may be one or zero, and the variables in the minimum candidate set are fixed to one. When generating an offspring solution, the variables in the maximum candidate set but out of the minimum candidate set are determined by its two parents.

The pseudocode of mining maximum candidate sets is presented in Algorithm 4.7, where the maximum candidate sets are initialized to those obtained in the previous mining operation. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are stored in (Line 1), and the dimensions that are zero in all the binary vectors in are eliminated from (Lines 2 and 3) and (Lines 4 and 5). To initialize more maximum candidate sets according to the current , half the binary vectors are selected from (Line 7) each time, and the dimensions that are nonzero in at least one of the selected binary vectors constitute a new initial maximum candidate set (Lines 8 and 9). After evaluating all the maximum candidate sets by Eq. (4.15) based on (Line 10), the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method iteratively evolves them by using the selection strategies of NSGA‐II (Lines 13 and 16) and the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 14). For the sake of efficiency, the number of candidate sets is set to 20 and the number of iterations is set to 10.

The pseudocode of mining minimum candidate sets is presented in Algorithm 4.8, which is very similar to the pseudocode of mining maximum candidate sets. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are stored in (Line 1), and the dimensions that are zero in all the binary vectors in are eliminated from (Lines 2 and 3) and (Lines 4 and 5). To initialize more minimum candidate sets according to the current , half the binary vectors are selected from (Line 7) each time, and the dimensions that are nonzero in all the selected binary vectors constitute a new initial minimum candidate set (Lines 8 and 9). After evaluating all the minimum candidate sets by Eq. (4.16) based on (Line 10), the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method iteratively evolves them by using the selection strategies of NSGA‐II (Lines 13 and 16) and the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 14).

4.4.3 Binary Genetic Operators of PM‐MOEA

After obtaining the maximum and minimum candidate sets by the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method, PM‐MOEA can generate the binary vectors of offspring solutions in the reduced binary search spaces. Different from MOEA/PSL that generates parts of the offspring solutions in the original decision space for alleviating prematurity, PM‐MOEA generates all the offspring solutions within the dimensions determined by the maximum candidate sets, since the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method provides multiple maximum and minimum candidate sets with good diversity, and one maximum candidate set and one minimum candidate set are randomly selected each time.

The pseudocode of offspring generation in PM‐MOEA is described in Algorithm 4.9, where two parents are used to generate one offspring solution each time. Before offspring generation, a maximum candidate set is randomly selected from (Line 9) and a minimum candidate set is randomly selected from (Line 11), where should be a subset of (Line 10). While if there does not exist any being a subset of any (Line 3), is randomly selected (Line 4) while is set to empty (Line 5). Then, the binary vectors of two parents are used to generate the binary vector of one offspring solution, and the real vectors of two parents are used to generate the real vector of one offspring solution (Line 12). The generation of binary vectors is implemented by the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 15), and the generation of real vectors is implemented by simulated binary crossover [10] and polynomial mutation [11] (Line 18). Besides, the binary variables out of are fixed to zero (Line 14) and the binary variables in are fixed to one (Line 16).

The binary genetic operators of PM‐MOEA aim to (a) equate the expectation of the number of flipped nonzero variables with the expectation of the number of flipped zero variables, and (b) keep the expectation of the total number of flipped variables unchanged. By doing so, the generated binary vectors are not expected to have the same number of zeros and ones, and the sparsity of offspring solutions can be ensured. Assuming that a binary vector having nonzero variables and zero variables is flipped with a probability of on each dimension, then holds for condition (a) and holds for condition (b), where denotes the probability of flipping each nonzero variable and denotes the probability of flipping each zero variable.
