4.4.4 Procedure of PM‐MOEA

With the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method and the binary genetic operators, the procedure of PM‐MOEA is presented in Algorithm 4.11. First, a population with solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), and the maximum candidate sets and minimum candidate sets are initialized to empty (Lines 3 and 4). At each generation, and are updated through the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method based on the current population (Lines 6 and 7), and the mating pool is constructed by selecting parents from the population via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers (Line 8). After that, offspring solutions are generated with the assistance of , , and the new binary genetic operators (Line 9). To select solutions from the combination of and , PM‐MOEA adopts the same environmental selection strategy as SparseEA and MOEA/PSL, where solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 10). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of PM‐MOEA, the time complexity is for frequent pattern mining, for offspring generation, and for environmental selection, where denotes the number of iterations for frequent pattern mining, denotes the maximum number of maximum and minimum candidate sets, denotes the number of decision variables, and denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of PM‐MOEA is .

4.5 Experimental Comparisons

To investigate the performance of SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA, they are compared with several representative MOEAs on benchmark and real‐world sparse LSMOPs. The compared MOEAs include a classical evolutionary algorithm NSGA‐II [6], two decision variable grouping‐based evolutionary algorithms MOEA/DVA [21] and LMEA [22], two decision space reduction‐based evolutionary algorithms WOF‐SMPSO [23] and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II [24], and a novel search strategy‐based evolutionary algorithm LMOCSO [25]. The tested sparse LSMOPs include the benchmark problems SMOP1–SMOP8 [7], the neural network training problem (including four test instances NN1–NN4 with different datasets) introduced in Eq. (2.23), and the frequent pattern mining problem (including four test instances PM1–PM4 with different datasets) introduced in Eq. (2.28). The population size is set to 100 and the number of function evaluations is set to , where is the number of decision variables ranging from 100 to 6241. The populations obtained on benchmark problems are assessed by IGD [26], and the populations obtained on real‐world problems are assessed by HV [27].

Table 4.2 lists the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold and the statistically similar ones are highlighted. It can be observed that the decision variable grouping‐based and novel search strategy‐based evolutionary algorithms (i.e., MOEA/DVA, LMEA, and LMOCSO) perform worse than the classical NSGA‐II, which indicates that these MOEAs are ineffective for solving sparse LSMOPs, though they are tailored for solving general LSMOPs. The decision space reduction‐based evolutionary algorithms (i.e., WOF‐SMPSO and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II) perform better, as they can converge to quasi‐optimal regions very quickly. The three sparse evolutionary algorithms (i.e., SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA) exhibit the best performance, which verifies the effectiveness of the strategies for finding sparse Pareto optimal solutions. More specifically, MOEA/PSL has the best overall performance on real‐coded problems (i.e., SMOP1–SMOP8 and NN1–NN4) since it uses RBM and DAE to reduce the dimensionality of both the binary vectors and real vectors, while PM‐MOEA has the best overall performance on binary‐coded problems (i.e., PM1–PM4), since it uses an evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to reduce the dimensionality of the binary vectors.

Moreover, Fig. 4.4 plots the populations with the median HV values obtained by the nine MOEAs on a neural network training problem, where the left axis shows the network complexity and training loss and the right axis shows the network complexity and test loss. Obviously, the solutions obtained by SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA have worse training loss but similar test loss to the solutions obtained by the other MOEAs, which indicates that the solutions obtained by the other MOEAs overfit the training samples due to their high complexities. As a consequence, it is reasonable to use sparse MOEAs to minimize both the network complexity and loss in training neural networks.

4.6 Summary

This chapter presents the first three MOEAs for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. The most significant feature of these MOEAs is that they search for the sparse Pareto optimal solutions of specific LSMOPs by customizing effective strategies, such as the population initialization strategy in SparseEA, the Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy in MOEA/PSL, and the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method in PM‐MOEA. Due to the wide application scenarios of sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, it appears as an emerging topic in evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, and an increasing number of new methods are being proposed [28–37].

In the following chapters, a number of large‐scale MOEAs tailored for the applications in several representative areas are presented, where each MOEA customizes novel strategies to tackle the difficulties of a specific application.

5
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization for Community Detection in Complex Networks

5.1 Introduction

The complex network is composed of a set of nodes and edges, where a node represents an item and an edge indicates that there is a relationship between the nodes connected by it. Fig. 5.1 gives an illustrative example of complex network. In the real world, there is a wide variety of complex systems that can be modeled as complex networks, such as social platforms, power systems, and World Wide Web. The community detection is to divide the nodes in a complex network into different groups, so that the nodes densely connect to the nodes in the same group (called community or cluster), but sparsely connect to the nodes in the other groups. In Fig. 5.1, the complex network can be divided into two communities. One is made up of nodes and the other is made up of nodes . The community detection is a vital analysis technique for revealing useful information hidden in complex networks. For example, in social networks, the communities are helpful to find a group of people with similar interests [1]. In protein–protein interaction networks, the communities can be used to identify the functional modules [2, 3]. In recent years, a large number of community detection algorithms have been proposed based on different ideas [4–6]. Generally, the existing algorithms tailored for community detection can be divided into three groups [7]. The first group adopts traditional methods in data clustering to merge densely connected nodes, such as hierarchical clustering [8] and spectral clustering [9]. The second group removes the edges that connect different communities to partition networks [10]. As for the third group, it resorts to optimization algorithms including mathematical programming [11] and heuristics [12], where the communities are determined by optimizing the metrics for the quality of communities.

As a meta‐heuristic algorithm, evolutionary algorithms have been successfully applied for community detection in complex networks, which can be divided into two categories according to the number of objectives to be optimized. In the first category, the communities are obtained by evolutionary algorithms to optimize a single objective, such as the modularity and edge betweenness. In the second category, the evolutionary algorithms simultaneously optimize multiple conflicting objectives to divide the nodes into different communities. Compared to single‐objective evolutionary algorithms, multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) have attracted more attention in complex networks for community detection. The main reasons are twofold. On the one hand, there exist some potential disadvantages in community detection by optimizing a single objective, such as the limited resolution of modularity. As pointed out in [13, 14], only optimizing the modularity might overlook the communities with small size, and empirical results indicate that multi‐objective optimization is an effective way to tackle this issue. On the other hand, different from single‐objective optimization, the MOEAs can find a set of Pareto optimal solutions rather than a single optimal solution in one run. Since each solution in the Pareto optimal set represents a trade‐off between the multiple objectives, the MOEA‐based community detection methods can provide a set of network partitions with different hierarchical levels, which means that this kind of methods is a rich framework for finding the hierarchical community structure of complex networks [15, 16].

Despite the promising performance achieved by MOEAs on community detection, most of the existing algorithms suffer from the scalability issue due to the curse of dimensionality. As analyzed in [17, 18], the search space of MOEAs increases exponentially with the increase of network size in community detection. This fact can naturally lead to most of the existing MOEA‐based algorithms being only suitable for networks having a relatively small number of nodes. To enhance the scalability of MOEAs in large‐scale complex networks, a number of ideas and/or strategies have been proposed for MOEA‐based community detection algorithms in recent years. In the following sections, two representative ideas tailored for MOEAs to detect communities in large‐scale complex networks will be presented, namely, the network reduction for multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (RMOEAs) and the parallel framework for multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (PMOEAs).

5.2 Network Reduction‐Based Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Community Detection

As discussed above, the main bottleneck of MOEAs for community detection in large‐scale complex networks lies in the curse of dimensionality. An intuitive idea is whether we can reduce the tremendous search space of MOEAs by utilizing the problem‐specific knowledge and information, i.e., those related to community detection and complex networks. Inspired by this idea, the network reduction‐based multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (RMOEA) was first suggested in [19], where two kinds of strategies are proposed to reduce the size of complex networks, namely, prereduction and reduction in evolution. These two strategies are based on the following observation. For a given complex network, there usually exist some nodes in the network that can easily be checked for belonging to the same community. The prereduction reduces the size of complex networks by simply checking the local topology structures, and the reduction in evolution achieves further reduction of networks by finding the local communities found during the evolution of MOEAs. The proposed RMOEA considers the local communities obtained by prereduction and reduction in evolution as a whole in later evolution of the algorithm. By doing so, the size of complex networks being handled is reduced; hence, the scalability of RMOEA to large‐scale complex networks can be considerately enhanced.

5.2.2 Prereduction Based on Local Network Topology Structure

As discussed above, some local communities can be easily identified by only checking the local topology structure of networks. Hence, the proposed RMOEA first reduces the size of complex networks according to the local topology structure of networks, before the evolution of population starts. The pseudocode of prereduction in RMOEA is given in Algorithm 5.1. To be specific, the prereduction is performed as follows.

First, the RMOEA randomly selects a node from the complex network , and determines a subgraph of (Lines 4–7). The subgraph consists of the nodes , (a neighboring node of which has the largest degree), (a neighboring node of which shares the largest number of neighbors with ), and all common neighbors of and . Then, the RMOEA extends the subgraph by adding some neighbors of (Lines 8–15). To ensure that these nodes belong to the same community, the RMOEA only adds each of the neighbors of whose number of links with is larger than one half of its degree. After that, the local communities of is determined, and the RMOEA merges all nodes in into one node to reduce the size of network being handled (Lines 16 and 17). The RMOEA will repeat to find the other local communities for the remaining nodes in the network and this process stops until all nodes of the network have been assigned to local communities.

Fig. 5.2 gives an illustrative example of prereduction developed in the RMOEA, where a network with seven nodes is considered, and we assume that the node 1 is selected to identify the corresponding local community. First, the subgraph {1,2,3,5} plotted in Fig. 5.2 (b) is obtained by the RMOEA, given that the node 3 is the neighbor of node 1 that owns the largest degree, and nodes 2 and 5 share the largest number of neighbors with node 3. Second, as depicted in Fig. 5.2, since all the links of node 4 are connected to subgraph {1, 2, 3, 5}, whereas for nodes 6 and 7 only half of links are connected to subgraph {1, 2, 3, 5}, the node 4 is added to the local community. Third, the RMOEA merges the local community {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} into one node, so that the network to be handled is reduced to a network with only three nodes.

5.2.3 Network Reduction in Evolution Based on Elite Individuals

In addition to the local topology structure, some local communities can also be obtained in evolution by using the elite individuals searched by MOEAs. In the proposed RMOEA, two metrics are employed to determine the elite individuals in population. One is the widely used metric for measuring the quality of found communities, namely, modularity . The larger the modularity is, the better quality the found communities have. The other is the number of communities . Considering that the a large implies that the size of each found community is small, it is helpful to reduce the probability of incorrectly identified local communities. The procedure of elite individual selection is presented in Algorithm 5.2. For a population , the modularity and the number of communities corresponding to each individual are first calculated, and the non‐dominated individuals are selected as the elite individuals for network reduction.

The pseudocode of network reduction based on elite individuals is presented in Algorithm 5.3. First, the elite individuals are selected from current population by using Algorithm 5.2. Then, the individual with the largest number of communities is selected from . Third, the individual is used to identify the local communities based on whether all the nodes in a community of belong to the same community in the remaining elite individuals. Specifically, for a community in , if all nodes in are identified as in one community by the remaining elite individuals, then is considered as a local community. Otherwise, the maximal subset of which are identified in one community by the remaining elite individuals is considered as a local community. The above operations repeat until all communities in are checked. Lastly, a reduced network is obtained by merging all nodes in each local community into one node in , and the population for the reduced network is obtained by merging the genes of nodes of each local community into one gene for all individuals in . For each individual, an index of the local community is assigned to the merged gene, and the community information on the rest genes in the individual keeps unchanged.

Fig. 5.3 plots an illustrative example of elite individual‐based network reduction. Fig. 5.3(a) displays the original complex network with seven nodes. In Fig. 5.3(b), it is assumed that the two elite individuals and have been selected from population for determining the local communities. Here, the individuals are represented by the locus‐based representation scheme, where each gene of the individual represents the index of a node that belongs to the same community. The partitions corresponding to and are shown in Fig. 5.3(c), where has four communities including {1, 2, 3, 4}, {5}, {6}, and {7}, and the partition of is {1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5}, {6}, and {7}. Since the number of communities in is larger than that in , the is used to obtain the local communities. For community {1, 2, 3}, it is identified as a local community since all of its nodes are identified as in one community by individual . For community {4}, it is also considered as a local community due to the fact that only one node is contained in the community. This is also the case for communities {5}, {6}, and {7}. In this way, five local communities {1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5}, {6}, and {7} are obtained from the elite individuals and , and the original complex network is reduced to a network with five nodes {, 4, 5, 6, 7} as displayed in Fig. 5.3(d). Here, the local community {1, 2, 3} is merged into one node . Accordingly, the and are changed to {, , 5, 6, 7} and {, 4, 5, 6, 7} as shown in Fig. 5.3(d), where is assigned to the merged gene and the information on the rest genes keeps unchanged.

5.2.4 Procedure of RMOEA

The procedure of RMOEA is described in Algorithm 5.4, where the framework of MOEA/D [22] is adopted to evolve the population. First, the RMOEA conducts the prereduction for complex network by using the local topology structure of network (Algorithm 5.1). Second, based on the network obtained by the pre‐reduction, the RMOEA initializes a population and a reference point . Here, the locus‐based adjacency encoding schema is used to generate the population , where each gene of individuals is first randomly assigned to an index of a neighbor of the node corresponding to this gene or index of the node itself, and then the genes in the individuals are iteratively replaced by the index shared by most of its neighbors, until the genes keep unchanged. For reference point , it is initialized as the best values of and in the population. Third, the RMOEA assigns individuals to each weight vector according to the Euclidean distance between the individuals and weight vectors. Fourth, the RMOEA further reduces the size of network by using elite individuals based on the network reduction in evolution. Specifically, for each generation satisfying , the reduced network is reduced by using elite individuals found during evolution (Algorithm 5.3). Here, is the modular operation and is a parameter controlling the number of reductions during evolution. Moreover, for each individual , the RMOEA randomly selects an individual from (a set of individuals assigned to the weight vector) to generate an offspring by crossover and mutation operators in each generation. The and reference point are updated according to the Tchebycheff value of the offspring. The details of crossover and mutation operations are given in Fig. 5.4. The RMOEA will repeat to evolve the population until the maximum number of generations is reached.

It is worth noting that the network reduction method might find incorrect local communities, which means that the local communities identified by the reduction in evolution may contain some nodes belonging to different communities. Hence, the RMOEA integrates a local community repairing strategy to correct the misidentified nodes in the reduced network. The pseudocode of the local community repairing strategy is elaborated in Algorithm 5.5. First, the set of elite individuals are selected from the population (Line 1). Second, for each elite individual in , the misidentified nodes are detected by checking whether the communities of contain some nodes belonging to different local communities. More specifically, a node is considered as misidentified one if a better modularity can be achieved by moving it to the communities of its neighbors. Last, the misidentified nodes are removed from the merged nodes of reduced network as a separate node, and the genes of the misidentified nodes are also added to each individual in population .

Fig. 5.5 shows an illustrative example of the local community repairing strategy. As plotted in Fig. 5.5(a), a local community {3, 5, 6, 7, 8} is identified by the elite individuals in the population, and only node 3 has at least one neighbor that does not belong to the local community. Furthermore, the modularity increases from 0.2219 to 0.3517, when node 3 is removed from the local community {3, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Hence, the local community is repaired as {5, 6, 7, 8}, by which the quality of local communities found by elite individuals can be considerably improved.

As presented in Algorithm 5.4, the RMOEA contains four main steps, network reduction based on the local topology, population initialization, network reduction based on the elite individuals, and population evolution. For the network reduction based on local topology, it holds a time complexity of since in the worst case, it needs the time complexity of to identify the local community for a given node. Here, is the maximum degree of nodes in the complex network. The population initialization takes the time complexity of , due to the fact that for each gene of individuals in the population, the maximum number of checking neighbors is . The time complexity of the network reduction based on elite individuals is . It is because that the most time‐consuming operation in this step is the calculation of modularity, which holds the time complexity of for each individual. As for the population evolution, its time complexity is , considering that in each generation, the RMOEA needs to calculate the values of the two objectives, and , which takes the time complexity of . 5.2.5 Experimental Comparisons

To verify the performance of RMOEA, it is compared with several representative community detection algorithms. The compared algorithms include five popular evolutionary algorithm‐based community detection algorithms, namely, CoCoMi [23], MOCD [13], MOGA‐net [16], MODTLBO/D [24], and MODPSO [14], where the CoCoMi is a single‐objective evolutionary algorithm, while the MOCD, MOGA‐net, MODTLBO/D, and MODPSO are MOEAs. Moreover, two non‐EA‐based community detection algorithms, namely, Louvain [25] and SSCF [9], are also employed as compared algorithms. The parameters of the compared algorithms are set to the values recommended in [14], which is also listed in Table 5.1. For the RMOEA, the number of reductions in evolution is set to 2 in the experiments.

The test datasets include synthetic benchmark networks and real‐world networks. The synthetic benchmark networks are LFR networks [26], which are widely used to verify the performance of community detection algorithms [6, 27]. The real‐world networks include ‐ and networks that are used in [28], and ‐, ‐, ‐, ‐ and ‐ that are collected by the Stanford Network Analysis Project [29]. Table 5.3 lists the experimental results of the RMOEA and seven compared algorithms, averaged over 20 runs on LFR benchmark networks with the nodes ranging from 10,000 to 50,000. The Wilcoxon rank sum test results with a significance level of 0.05 are also given at the bottom of the table. From Table 5.3, it can be found that the RMOEA owns better scalability than the other five evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms. Compared to non‐EA‐based algorithms, although the efficiency of RMOEA is worse than Louvain, the detection performance of RMOEA is significantly better than that of Louvain. Despite that the SSCF shows a better detection performance than RMOEA on the LRF networks with 10,000 and 20,000 nodes, it cannot obtain results within 12 hours on the other networks. Different from the SSCF, the RMOEA can always obtain community results within reasonable runtime on all sizes of LFR networks, and achieve competitive detection performance.

Table 5.4 gives the experimental results of the community detection algorithms averaged over 20 runs on seven real‐world networks. In Table 5.4, the Louvain achieves the best computational efficiency on all seven real‐world networks. The RMOEA also holds a competitive efficiency, which is much better than the other five evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms. In terms of detection performance, the RMOEA owns the best overall performance. It achieves the best on five of seven networks. Based on the above experimental comparison, it can be concluded that the RMOEA is a promising community detection algorithm for large‐scale networks, in terms of detection performance and runtime.

5.3 Parallel Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Community Detection

Parallelization is a widely adopted technique to enhance the scalability of evolutionary algorithms in tackling large‐scale optimization problems. The idea of parallelization has also adopted for community detection in large‐scale complex networks. Based on this idea, a parallel multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm called PMOEA is reported in [27]. In the PMOEA, several key nodes of a complex network are first identified, and then the communities associated with these key nodes are parallel detected by MOEAs. After that, a single‐objective evolutionary algorithm is employed to integrate the communities associated with the key nodes, by which the communities of the entire network are obtained. Since the communities associated with the key nodes are detected in parallel, the efficiency of PMOEA in handling large‐scale complex networks can be significantly improved. The framework of PMOEA is presented in Fig. 5.6 and the pseudocode is given in Algorithm 5.6.

5.3.1 Key Node Identification

The pseudocode of identifying key nodes is given in Algorithm 5.7, which consists of the following steps. First, the average degree of all nodes in is calculated. Next, the nodes that own degree larger than the average degree are determined and added into the set . All nodes with the maximum degree are considered as key nodes in . Then, the nodes with the maximum degree and all other nodes that have at least one edge with these nodes are removed from the . Among the remaining nodes in , those with the maximum degree are also considered as key nodes. This process is repeated until no node remains in set . It is necessary to stress that the key nodes of a network can also be identified by other effective strategies.

5.3.2 Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Detecting the Communities Associated with a Key Node

After identifying key nodes of a network, the PMOEA will detect the communities associated with these key nodes in parallel. To this end, an MOEA is devised based on the decomposition‐based MOEA (MOEA/D) [22], which detects a community of a key node by simultaneously minimizing the following two objectives.

Since the MOEA only detects the communities associated with a key node instead of all communities in the complex network, the dedicated crossover and mutation operators need to be devised to guide the evolution of population, which are described as follows.

5.3.3 Evolutionary Algorithm for Determining the Communities of the Entire Network

After detecting the communities associated with all key nodes, the PMOEA will obtain the communities of the entire network based on these detected communities. Due to the fact that the MOEA returns a set of communities for each key node, the PMOEA employs an evolutionary algorithm to select a suitable community from the set of communities detected for each key node and then constitutes the community partition of the entire network by using the selected communities. The pseudocode of evolutionary algorithm for determining the community partition of the entire network is presented in Algorithm 5.9.

The second and third steps will be repeated until the maximum number of generations is reached. Fourth, the community partition of the entire network is improved by using the following strategy. 5.3.5 Experimental Comparisons

To verify the performance of PMOEA, it is compared to eight algorithms tailored for community detection. For these compared algorithms, six of them are evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms, namely, CoCoMi [23], MOCD [13], MOGA‐net [16], MODPSO [14], QDM‐PSO [34], and PaGeCoDe [35], and two of them are non‐EA‐based algorithms including LET [36] and FOCS [37]. The parameters of these algorithms are set to the values recommended in the original references, which are also listed in Table 5.5. It is worth noting that in the MOEA of PMOEA, the crossover and mutation probabilities are set to 0.9 and 0.6, respectively, and in the EA of PMOEA, the crossover and mutation probabilities are set to 0.6 and 0.01, respectively. Moreover, the parameter in PMOEA for merging two communities is set to 0.4 in the experiments.

Two groups of complex networks are used to verify the detection performance of different algorithms. The first group is the synthetic networks which are generated by using the LFR model [26] with nodes ranging from 50,000 to 200,000. The second group is the real‐world networks, including five networks from the Stanford large network dataset [29], namely, ca‐HepTh2, ca‐AstroPh, ca‐CondMat, loc‐Brightkite, and loc‐Gowalla. The details of these networks are given in Table 5.6. The evaluation metric used for synthetic networks is the since the ground truth of these networks is known, and the modularity () is adopted for real‐world networks due to the fact that most of them do not have a known ground truth.

Table 5.7 presents the detection performance of the PMOEA and the eight compared algorithms on LFR benchmark networks with a size ranging from 50,000 to 200,000. The Wilcoxon rank‐sum test results with a significance level of 0.05 are also given at the bottom of the tables. From Table 5.7, it can be found that the PMOEA achieves the best detection quality on all LFR networks. On the contrary, most of the evolutionary algorithm‐based compared algorithms cannot obtain results within 17 hours. Although the FOCS owns higher computational efficiency than PMOEA, the detection quality is much worse than PMOEA. Table 5.8 lists the detection quality of different algorithms on five real‐world networks, where the PMOEA also holds the best value of . As for the other evolutionary algorithm‐based community detection algorithms, although some of them can complete within 17 hours, the value of their detection results is worse than that of PMOEA. The non‐EA‐based algorithm FOCS consumes less computational time than PMOEA, but its detection quality is inferior to that of the PMOEA. Hence, it can be concluded that the PMOEA owns a good scalability for large‐scale complex networks in terms of both efficiency and detection performance.

5.4 Summary

This chapter presents two ideas of enhancing the scalability of MOEAs in solving the community detection problems for large‐scale complex networks, and two MOEAs, namely, RMOEA and PMOEA, are developed based on the ideas. The RMOEA utilizes the local communities detected during the evolution to reduce the size of complex networks, so that the scalability of MOEA to large‐scale complex networks can be considerately enhanced. The PMOEA is based on the idea of parallelization to tackle large‐scale complex networks, where the community detection of the entire network is decomposed into detecting the communities associated with a number of key nodes performed in parallel. Although the reduction and parallelization are two widely used technologies for large‐scale optimization, there are many other technologies that can be used to deal with large‐scale optimization, such as decomposition [38] and search enhancement [39, 40]. In the following chapters, a number of MOEAs with different strategies to tackle the large‐scale optimization in other applications are presented.

6
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Logistics Scheduling

6.1 Introduction

Logistics has been known as an important foundation of worldwide economic development and thus widely exists in social life [1]. A good logistics scheduling plan guarantees that the materials flow fluently in a logistics system and significantly contributes to economic growth [2]. Hence, logistics scheduling remains a hot research field over decades, which involves a large variety of optimization problems: facility location, vehicle routing, and container loading, to name a few [3–5]. A large number of algorithms have been developed to address these optimization problems, which are roughly categorized into two groups: exact algorithms and heuristic ones. Exact algorithms often formulate logistics scheduling problems as mathematical programming models that can be iteratively computed, such as linear programming models or dynamic programming models [6]. Heuristic algorithms iteratively seek optimal solutions in the search space of logistics scheduling problems in a flexible way [7]. Exact algorithms are often able to obtain the optimal solution of a small‐scale single‐objective logistics scheduling problem at an acceptable computational cost. Nevertheless, they can barely obtain high‐quality solutions for a large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problem, which typically formulates a multi‐objective problem as a single‐objective optimization model by a weighted method and neglects a potential conflict between multiple objectives. Thereafter, heuristic algorithms are developed to solve multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems due to their capability of simultaneously optimizing multiple objectives, which, however, still have difficulty in addressing large‐scale multi‐objective problems. Due to the NP‐hard characteristic of many logistics scheduling problems, a large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problem generally has a huge solution search space, which hinders many existing heuristic algorithms from obtaining satisfying solutions at an acceptable computational cost.

Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are a type of popular metaheuristic algorithms and have exhibited good performance in addressing multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems [8, 9]. Due to the fact that EAs are population‐based searching methods, they are able to simultaneously optimize multiple objectives by searching in multiple directions in the decision space. Nevertheless, it is still difficult for EAs to handle large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems, since the performance of an EA considerably deteriorates with the rapid growth of problem size. This motivates many researchers to improve EAs for large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems, and this chapter presents two state‐of‐the‐art EAs for two typical large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems: an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping‐based heuristic algorithm (EMRG‐HA) for the vehicle routing problem (VRP) [10] and a clustering‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA with reference point adaptation (AR‐MOEA+SA) for the facility location problem (FLP) [4]. The VRP presented in this chapter is the classic and basic capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), which serves as a reliable testbed for many VRP optimization algorithms. The FLP presented in this chapter is a real‐world application in emergency management: the uncertain shelter location problem (USLP).

6.2 Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Route Grouping‐Based Heuristic Algorithm for Large‐Scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems

The task of a typical CVRP is to plan the optimal traveling routes with the lowest traveling cost for a fleet of vehicles so as to serve a set of customers with known demands, where all the vehicles are assumed to be homogeneous and thus have the same capacity. The large‐scale capacitated vehicle routing problem (LSCVRP) refers to the CVRP with thousands of customers to be served, which is challenging and draws much attention from CVRP researchers [11–14]. Particularly, the idea of divide‐and‐conquer has been widely used in developing large‐scale optimization algorithms by decomposing a large‐scale optimization problem into some small sub‐components that can be easily and independently solved [15, 16]. In the field of large‐scale logistics scheduling, the idea of divide‐and‐conquer is mainly used in two ways: to geographically decompose customers into groups of customers [17, 18] or to decompose routes into groups of routes for service of different vehicles [19, 20]. Regardless of the studies that use divide‐and‐conquer for LSCVRPs, many of these studies fail to produce a good decomposition for either customers or routes [18, 21]. The customer‐decomposition strategies could easily result in that customers served by the same vehicles in the optimal routes cannot be divided into a group, since the customers are divided into groups based on their geographical locations. For the route‐decomposition strategies, they are often hard to achieve a good decomposition since the clustering of routes is more difficult than the clustering of customers, especially for the definition of intraclustering and interclustering distances for routes.

Thereafter, this section presents a divide‐and‐conquer‐based heuristic algorithm EMRG‐HA for solving LSCVRPs, which reports an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping method to achieve promising decomposition for LSCVRPs [22]. By exploiting the advantage of evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, the route grouping method mathematically formulates a typical CVRP as a tri‐objective model by simultaneously optimizing the intra‐group similarity, inter‐group similarity and inter‐group balance. The three objectives guide the optimization of LSCVRPs to find high‐quality route groupings with low inter‐group similarity, high intra‐group similarity and inter‐group balance. Because of the fact that route groupings have a great influence on the quality of routes, the high‐quality route groupings thus can lead to high‐quality routes in the optimization of LSCVRPs.

In the following, we first present the formal definition of CVRP, then the EMRG‐HA for solving LSCVRPs is elaborated. Finally, experimental comparisons between the EMRG‐HA and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for CVRPs are presented and discussed.

6.2.2 Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Route Grouping Method

To obtain promising route groupings, EMRG‐HA uses an evolutionary tri‐objective optimization‐based route grouping method, termed EMRG, in the optimization of LSCVRPs. The three optimization objectives, namely, the intra‐group similarity, the inter‐group similarity and inter‐group balance, are adopted to guarantee that the EMRG finds promising route groupings in the optimization of LSCVRPs. Specifically, minimizing the intra‐group similarity ensures that the routes in the same group are similar enough to be served by the same vehicle, while maximizing the inter‐group similarity enables that the routes in different groups are different enough from each other to be served by different vehicles. Minimizing the inter‐group balance makes sure that EMRG achieves balanced route groupings so as to adapt the use of vehicles. Formally, the three optimization objectives are defined as follows.

Therefore, there is no need to adopt a mutation operator in EMRG.

6.2.3 Framework of EMRG‐HA

Figure 6.2 illustrates the overall procedure of EMRG‐HA that integrates the evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping into the search process for solving LSCVRPs. As can be observed from the figure, integrating the route grouping into the search process guarantees that the route groupings can be flexibly adapted and updated based on route quality, due to the fact that the intra‐group similarity, inter‐group similarity, and inter‐group balance are continuously optimized for subsequent promising groupings. Furthermore, the route quality is in return improved with the quality improvement of grouping during the optimization process. More detailed steps of EMRG‐HA are presented in Algorithm 6.3, which mainly consists of three steps.

First, EMRG‐HA randomly generates a solution of the CVRP so that all the vehicles satisfy capacity constraint. For a CVRP with customers, EMRG‐HA encodes a solution as , where , , is a route for the th vehicle, denote the customers served by the th vehicle satisfying that , and is the number of vehicles used in solution . Second, EMRG‐HA performs the evolutionary multi‐objective optimization‐based route grouping method EMRG to produce a set of groupings for routes of solution . Third, EMRG‐HA conducts the tabu search based local search in the produced route groupings so as to improve the quality of solution . The same operations for the improved solution in the above two steps will repeat until the termination criterion of EMRG‐HA is satisfied. Otherwise, the obtained solution will be output as the final solution for the LSCVRP. With the improvement of solution quality during the evolution, the EMRG‐HA is able to dynamically adapt the ingredients of decomposed subcomponents in the search process via the route grouping.

For the route grouping in each solution, a tabu search‐based local search (TS‐LS) is employed to improve the route quality in the groups of the grouping, which is presented in Algorithm 6.2. First, the TS‐LS randomly selects groupings from , where is used to control the number of groupings for reducing computational cost of TS‐LS. Second, for each of the randomly selected groupings, the TS‐LS selects one group via the roulette wheel method to apply local search to customers in the group. Third, TS‐LS applies the tabu search to improve the route quality for each of the selected groups, where three operators: single insertion, swap, and 2‐opt, are randomly selected for route quality improvement. The local search is performed for times for one group of routes. Finally, the routes improved by tabu search replace those in the selected group and a new solution thus is obtained for each grouping.

6.2.4 Experimental Comparisons

This section verifies the competitiveness of EMRG‐HA by comparing it with five state‐of‐the‐art algorithms for addressing LSCVRPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

The comparisons utilize two commonly used benchmark test sets for LSCVRPs: a set of 20 LSCVRP benchmark instances suggested by Golden et al. in [25] ranging from 240 to 483 customers (denoted as G1 to G20), and a set of 12 benchmark instances suggested by Li et al. in [26] ranging from 560 to 1200 customers (denoted as L1 to L12). Five existing heuristic algorithms for solving LSCVRPs are used as compared algorithms of EMRG‐HA, namely, hybrid genetic search with adaptive diversity control (HGSADC) [27], cooperative parallel metaheuristic (CPM) [28], parallel random record‐to‐record (PRRTR) [29], fixed‐J quantum annealing (FJ‐QA) [30], and variable neighbourhood simulated annealing (VNSA) [31]. All the parameters of each of the compared algorithms are set to the same values that are suggested in their original references. For EMRG‐HA, the maximum number of iterations is set to 30. For EMRG in EMRG‐HA, the population size is set to 50 and the maximum number of iterations is set to 100. Table 6.2 presents the parameter settings in EMRG‐HA. For fair comparisons, all algorithms are programmed in Matlab and executed on the CPU Intel Core i5‐7500 with 3.4 GHz and 16 GB memory.

Tables 6.3 and 6.4 present the best traveling cost achieved by EMRG‐HA and 5 compared algorithms on 20 test instances of Golden et al. and 12 test instances of Li et al. over 20 independent runs, in which the best values achieved by the compared algorithms refer to their original references. The best‐known traveling cost for each instance is given in Tables 6.3 and 6.4 and the result for each algorithm represents the gap between the result achieved by the algorithm and the best‐known result. Hence, the result 0 means that the algorithm achieves the best‐known result, and “+” (“”) indicates that the value is worse (better) than the best‐known result.

It can be observed from Tables 6.3 and 6.4 that EMRG‐HA can achieve the best‐known traveling cost on most LSCVRP test instances. Specifically, EMRG‐HA achieves the best‐known traveling cost on 16 of 20 Golden test instances, and it achieves the best‐known traveling cost on 7 instances of 12 Li test instances. Furthermore, EMRG‐HA produces a new best result on some test instances in comparison with the current best‐known result, i.e., the instance (G10) in Golden et al. benchmarks and the instance (L12) in Li et al. benchmarks. Thereafter, it can be concluded that the performance of EMRG‐HA is overall superior over five compared algorithms on the 32 LSCVRP test instances. Both HGSADC and CPM also have a competitive performance, despite that they fail to find a low traveling cost in a few instances, such as instances L2 and L5. It can be also found in Tables 6.3 and 6.4 that EMRG‐HA is computationally efficient in addressing LSCVRPs. To this end, EMRG‐HA is competitive in solving LSCVRPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

6.3 Clustering‐Based Surrogate‐Assisted Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Shelter Location Problem Under Uncertainty of Road Networks

Over the years, the USLP has attracted many researchers from a variety of fields due to its importance in tackling the threat of natural disasters, such as earthquakes, hurricanes, and tsunamis [32, 33]. There are two tasks for a shelter location problem, namely, selecting sites for shelter construction and assigning evacuees to shelters [34, 35]. The two tasks are obviously in conflict with each other since it is expected that less construction cost can be used to achieve a smaller evacuation distance from residential communities to shelters. The large‐scale uncertain shelter location problem (LSUSLP) refers to the USLP that contains hundreds of residential communities to be assigned, which is difficult to solve because it is computationally expensive to evaluate a solution for a USLP. One solution evaluation needs to compute the average traveling cost over a set of simulated damage scenarios. Since EAs are population‐based optimization algorithms, it will cost much computational budget to evaluate solutions at each generation of an EA optimization. Regardless of the wide applications of EAs in solving FLPs, few studies have been reported for LSUSLPs by using EAs [36–38].

This section introduces a surrogate‐assisted EA, termed AR‐MOEA+SA, for efficiently addressing LSUSLPs by using a surrogate modeling strategy [39]. The surrogate modeling strategy helps create computationally cheap function evaluation that well approximates the computationally expensive exact function evaluation, to replace the exact evaluation with the approximate one. In this case, the computational efficiency of solving LSUSLPs can be significantly improved to obtain high‐quality solutions for LSUSLPs at a low computational cost.

In this section, we first give the mathematical formulation of USLP, then the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method and framework of ARMOEA+SA are detailed. Finally, experimental comparisons between AR‐MOEA+SA and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for USLPs are presented and comparison results are discussed.

6.3.1 Problem Formulation

The task of USLP is to select a set of shelters from candidate shelters for construction, to achieve that the traveling distance between evacuees and selected shelters are shortest in both undamage and damage road network scenarios, and the shelter construction cost is as low as possible. It is assumed that there are candidate shelters, residential communities and a defined road network between candidate shelters and communities. Each road in the defined road network holds a probability to be broken, and the probability for each road is generally obtained based on properties of the road, such as the collapse resistance and quality of buildings along the road, etc. The notations used in the USLP formulation are presented in Table 6.5, and the USLP is formulated as follows:

(6.6)

where the operator denotes the OR operator, indicates that the th community is assigned to the th candidate shelter in the undamage (or th damage) scenario and 0 otherwise.

The three optimization objectives minimize the construction area for the selected shelters, the total evacuation distance in the undamage scenario, and that in the damage scenario, respectively. The objective is computationally expensive since the roads in the road network will be randomly damaged under their breaking probability in the damage scenario. Hence, a number of damage scenarios are necessary for estimating the evacuation distance in the damage scenario in one individual evaluation.

The constraints of USLP are listed as follows:

(6.7)

where indicates the maximum traveling distance for the th community. The first constraint ensures that the population assigned to each shelter does not exceed the capacity of the shelter, the second constraint guarantees that the traveling distance of each community is equal to or smaller than the maximum distance, and the third constraint represents that each community will be exactly assigned to one shelter.

6.3.2 Clustering‐Based Surrogate Modeling Method

The AR‐MOEA+SA utilizes a surrogate modeling method to conduct computationally cheap function evaluation which approximates the original computationally expensive exact one. Surrogates are a popular method to replace time‐consuming exact function evaluations in an EA optimization and thus leads to significant efficiency improvement of EA optimization. Nevertheless, it is difficult for most existing surrogate‐assisted EAs to accurately train a surrogate model with hundreds of dimensions, since training a high‐dimensional high‐accuracy surrogate model needs a very large amount of training data which are often hard to obtain in optimization process of EAs. Hence, AR‐MOEA+SA adopts a clustering‐based surrogate modeling method to transform the high‐dimensional LSUSLP decision variables into low‐dimensional ones before training a surrogate model, which effectively approximates original function evaluation and guarantees high efficiency in addressing LSUSLPs.

The procedure of the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method is shown in Fig. 6.3. The surrogate modeling method first selects non‐dominated individuals from current population via non‐dominated sorting. Next, the surrogate modeling method uses a clustering‐based strategy on the non‐dominated individuals in order to convert them into data points of low dimensions. Then, the surrogate modeling method updates the training data using the converted data points and an RBF network model is built by training on data. Finally, the surrogate modeling method uses the built RBF network model to evaluate the offsprings reproduced from current parent population. Note that here the clustering‐based strategy is also used to convert the offsprings into individuals of low dimensions, which is presented in Algorithm 6.4. Much sample data are necessary for effective surrogate modeling, which may be not affordable since the USLP generally holds hundreds of decision variables. Hence, a clustering‐based strategy is suggested in AR‐MOEA+SA to build the surrogate model at a low computational budget via converting the modeling of high dimensions into the one of low dimensions for the USLP. Specifically, Fig. 6.4 illustrates the process of building a surrogate model by clustering. The candidate shelters are clustered into multiple groups based on the geography locations of shelters. For each individual found in AR‐MOEA+SA optimization, the residential communities are covered by the groups according to the shelter coverage situation in the individual. This is because of the fact that the residential communities covered by one group are often assigned to another shelter in the same group if they cannot be evacuated to the original assigned shelter in a damage scenario. The assignment of communities in each group can thus be regarded as a whole that is represented by the total evacuation distance in this group.

The surrogate model built using the above method should be continuously updated, due to the fact that a fixed surrogate model often works only in the cases where the decision space has very low dimensions and the training data used in the surrogate modeling is quite sufficient. The surrogate update also refers to model management in surrogate‐assisted EAs, which needs to handle two issues: when is the surrogate updated and which individuals in current population are selected for updating the surrogate. Specifically, Algorithm 6.5 presents the pseudocode of model management in the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method.

6.3.3 Procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA

Based on the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method, AR‐MOEA+SA uses a state‐of‐the‐art multi‐objective EA, termed AR‐MOEA that is proposed in [40]. The AR‐MOEA is an indicator‐based multi‐objective EA using a performance indicator of inverted generational distance with noncontributing solution detection IGD‐NS [40]. Specifically, Algorithm 6.6 shows the procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA, which employs the radial basis function (RBF) as the surrogate model and adopts the Gaussian function as the basis function for RBF network. There are six main steps in the procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA.

First, AR‐MOEA+SA performs the initialization of population and surrogate model, which uses the clustering strategy to convert the initial population into initial training data for surrogate modeling. Based on the initial training data, a surrogate model is built and an archive is created to store all individuals under exact evaluations. Second, AR‐MOEA+SA performs the uniform crossover and mutation to produce offsprings from current parent population. Third, AR‐MOEA+SA uses the latest surrogate model to approximately evaluate each individual in the offspring population. Fourth, AR‐MOEA+SA utilizes the environmental selection in AR‐MOEA to select the parent population in next generation, which is based on the approximate evaluation results of individuals to be selected. Fifth, AR‐MOEA+SA updates the surrogate model according to the model management method presented in Algorithm 6.5, and the training data and the archive are also updated. The second to the fifth steps repeat until the termination criterion is satisfied. Finally, AR‐MOEA+SA averagely reevaluates the individuals from the archive on a set of 100 randomly generated damage scenarios so as to alleviate the influence of randomness. The non‐dominated individuals that are identified based on the reevaluations are obtained from the archive and regarded as the final result achieved by AR‐MOEA+SA.

6.3.4 Experimental Comparisons

In this section, we evaluate the performance of AR‐MOEA+SA in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency by comparing it with four state‐of‐the‐art algorithms for USLPs.

A set of four USLP test instances are used as test instances for all the compared algorithms, which consist of three simulated numerical instances and one real case. Particularly, three simulated test instances are created on the basis of the parameter settings in Table 6.6, in which the community scale varies from small, medium to large. Four compared algorithms are utilized for comparisons with AR‐MOEA+SA, namely, a mathematical programming method BD [33], an EA MNSGA‐II [41], a surrogate‐based optimization algorithm SA‐COSO [42], and AR‐MOEA without the surrogate modeling method [40].

The population size for AR‐MOEA+SA is set to 100, while the two sub‐populations in SA‐COSO/MNSGA‐II are set to hold 80 individuals and 20 ones, respectively. Each algorithm that uses uniform crossover and mutation operators holds a crossover probability of 0.8 and a mutation probability of , where is the number of decision variables. For RBF in AR‐MOEA+SA, the size of hidden nodes is set to 6, and the scale of training data is set to , in which indicates the data dimension. The results for each of MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA are obtained after 20 independent runs of the corresponding algorithm. All the experiments are performed on a PC with a 3.40 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU 6700 and the Windows 7 SP1 64 bit operating system.

Table 6.7 presents the evacuation distances obtained by five compared algorithms on the four instances, averaging over 20 independent runs. For highlighting the performance of AR‐MOEA+SA, three non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms BD, AR‐MOEA, and MNSGA‐II are performed for 20,000 exact function evaluations, while two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms AR‐MOEA+SA and SA‐COSO are performed for 2000 exact function evaluations.

It can be observed from Table 6.7 that AR‐MOEA+SA overall achieves the best performance in terms of the evacuation distances for both the undamage and damage scenarios on all test instances in comparison with four compared algorithms. Furthermore, AR‐MOEA+SA also uses the smallest shelter construction cost on all instances. Considering that the above results of AR‐MOEA+SA are obtained after only 2000 exact evaluations, AR‐MOEA+SA in fact achieves the best performance on all instances by using significantly less computational cost in comparison with non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms BD, MNSGA‐II, and AR‐MOEA.

For a deeper insight into the computational efficiency of AR‐MOEA, Table 6.8 lists the runtime(s) of four compared algorithms and AR‐MOEA+SA on four instances, where three non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms still are performed for 20,000 exact evaluations, and two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms are performed for 2000 exact ones. It can be seen from the table that the two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms AR‐MOEA+SA and SA‐COSO achieve the highest computational efficiency on all instances in comparison with the other three non‐surrogate‐assisted ones. This is because of the fact that the two surrogate‐assisted algorithms use a considerable number of computationally efficient approximate evaluations to replace computationally expensive ones during their evolution, which thus leads to high computational efficiency of the two algorithms.

Furthermore, Fig. 6.5 shows the number of exact function evaluations performed by AR‐MOEA, MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA on four instances with the growth of running generations. It can be observed from Fig. 6.5 that the two non‐surrogate‐assisted algorithms AR‐MOEA and MNSGA‐II perform much more exact evaluations than the two surrogate‐assisted algorithms SA‐COSO and AR‐MOEA+SA when they are in the same generations. This further validates that AR‐MOEA+SA is efficient in addressing computationally expensive LSUSLPs.

It can also be seen from Fig. 6.5 that AR‐MOEA+SA performs more exact evaluations than the other surrogate‐assisted algorithm SA‐COSO when they are at the same generations. Nevertheless, AR‐MOEA+SA contrarily takes less runtime than SA‐COSO on all instances, which is exhibited in Fig. 6.6. The reason lies in the fact that the surrogate model training of AR‐MOEA+SA consumes much less time than that of SA‐COSO during their evolution. The surrogate model training of SA‐COSO assists in creating approximate evaluations that have much cheaper computational cost than exact ones, which is, however, relatively more expensive than the model training of AR‐MOEA+SA. As a result, it is still necessary to develop surrogate‐assisted EAs that simultaneously hold high model precision and cheap training cost.

In summary, it can be drawn from the comparison results that AR‐MOEA+SA is an effective and efficient optimization algorithm for solving LSUSLPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

6.4 Summary

This chapter presents a CVRP optimization algorithm and a USLP optimization algorithm for solving LSCVRPs and USLPs, respectively. Specifically, a divide‐and‐conquer‐based heuristic algorithm, EMRG‐HA is introduced for solving LSCVRPs, where an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping method called EMRG is developed to perform the grouping of a set of given routes. The competitiveness of EMRG‐HA has also been empirically verified by comparing it with five existing heuristic algorithms for LSCVRPs in terms of both computational efficiency and solution quality.

A clustering‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA, termed AR‐MOEA+SA, is detailed for addressing USLPs. To build an effective surrogate model for the LSUSLP, in the AR‐MOEA+SA, a clustering‐based strategy is developed to convert the surrogate modeling of high‐dimensional problem into one of low‐dimensional problem. Comparison with four state‐of‐the‐art facility location optimization algorithms demonstrates the superiority of AR‐MOEA+SA in effectively and efficiently addressing USLPs.

7
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Power Systems

7.1 Introduction

Power systems are becoming increasingly complex due to rapid advancements in technology and the growing need for efficient, reliable, and sustainable energy management. This complexity is further intensified by the integration of renewable energy sources, distributed generation, and smart grid technologies. Managing and optimizing power systems necessitate addressing multiple objectives simultaneously, as various aspects of system performance, such as power generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption, are often interconnected and interdependent.

In order to effectively tackle these challenges, advanced optimization techniques are required that can capture the intricate relationships between multiple objectives and provide high‐quality solutions for the diverse array of problems encountered in power systems. Evolutionary algorithms are population‐based meta‐heuristics optimization algorithms, which are capable of obtaining a set of trade‐off solutions in a single run and less vulnerable to local optima. In the past few decades, evolutionary algorithms have demonstrated remarkable success in solving multi‐objective optimization problems across a wide range of domains. However, their performance usually deteriorates considerably when they are used to address large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (LSMOPs), which is attributed to the curse of dimensionality. In fact, the curse of dimensionality is also widely present in power systems. After all, the optimization problems in power systems usually have tens of thousands of or even more decision variables to be optimized.

This chapter presents an in‐depth exploration of evolutionary algorithms applied to power systems, with a particular focus on a case study involving the ratio error estimation of voltage transformers (VTs). In the case study, first, we discuss the importance of ratio error estimation of VTs and the limitations of existing methods. Then, we introduce the time‐varying ratio error estimation (TREE) method as an innovative solution to address the shortcomings of existing methods. Next, we present a data‐driven approach for formulating the TREE problem as a LSMOP, detailing the process of extracting statistical and physical principles from power distribution systems. Finally, a problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm is designed to solve the TREE problems, demonstrating the potential of evolutionary algorithms in addressing complex real‐world problems in power systems.

7.2 Ratio Error Estimation of Voltage Transformers

7.2.1 Problem Introduction

VTs are fundamental devices widely employed in industrial power delivery systems, particularly in substations, for measuring voltage values.

The ratio error (RE) of a VT can be mathematically expressed as [5]

(7.1)

where represents the primary voltage value measured by the VT, and (always unknown) denotes the corresponding true primary voltage value. Figure 7.1 displays the diagram of a representative 110 kV substation with four sets of three‐phase VTs in the power delivery system. Specifically, VT‐1 and VT‐2 measure the same three‐phase primary voltage values in parallel, while VT‐3 and VT‐4 measure the same three‐phase secondary voltage values in parallel. Consequently, the four VTs interact through the true voltage values. For example, VT‐1 and VT‐2 measure the same primary voltage value, while VT‐3 and VT‐4 measure the same secondary voltage value. Since the primary side voltage value is proportional to the secondary side voltage value, VT‐1 and VT‐2 are related to VT‐3 and VT‐4. Meanwhile, we denote the primary and secondary voltage values obtained by the th set of VTs as and , respectively. In this substation, the RE can be calculated based on one of the primary voltage values, such as , , or .

To obtain the REs of VTs, there are primarily two types of methods: calibration methods and data‐driven estimation methods. Calibration is conducted by de‐energizing the power and manually comparing the uncalibrated VT with the standard one [6]. Typical methods include off‐line and on‐site calibrations [7–9]. In contrast, data‐driven estimation methods construct specific models of the VTs and estimate the REs based on constraints derived from the electrical relationship and data collected from VTs, such as the adaptive detection method [10] and the line parameter estimation method [11]. However, both calibration and data‐driven estimation methods suffer from practical deficiencies. While calibration methods provide accurate REs under standard working conditions, they are expensive in terms of time and cost and must be used periodically [6]. For instance, most substations conduct calibration every four years or even longer, resulting in economic losses (e.g., over 0.3 million CNY) and taking a long time (e.g., more than one day) [12]. As for data‐driven estimation methods, despite their lower cost, their accuracy and versatility are unsatisfactory due to the limitations of the VT‐specific models [13, 14].

To address the challenges associated with existing calibration and data‐driven methods, Section 7.2.2 will introduce an innovative method that formulates the TREE problem as an LSMOP by taking into account the differences between the true voltage values and those measured by the VTs. Similar to calibration, the primary goal of the formulated problem is to estimate the true voltage values. The proposed method offers significant advantages over calibration and data‐driven error estimation methods, including reduced costs and enhanced versatility.

7.2.2.2 Objective Functions

The TREE problem involves three objective functions, which are formulated based on the relationship between the true voltage values and the measurements obtained from the VTs. A smaller objective value implies a better estimation accuracy for each objective function.

7.2.2.3 Constraint Functions

In a power delivery system, VTs in the same substation are connected through conductors, and the measurement of voltage and phase angle values is a long‐term process. Therefore, three main constraints can be formulated to restrict the feasible area of the problem: topology constraint, time series constraint, and phase constraint.

(1) Topology constraints

Topology constraints are derived from the three‐phase balance principle, stating that the true three‐phase primary voltages should be kept in balance if the grid is under control [15]. This balance is described by the voltage unbalance factor (VUF), which indicates the balance between three‐phase impedance. Since the three‐phase impedance is balanced and varies slowly (especially in the high‐voltage grid) [16], the VUF value and its fluctuation can be limited within a range as
