With the objective functions and constraints established, the TREE problems can be solved using evolutionary algorithms. The goal is to obtain the best estimation of the true voltage values and phase angles, while satisfying the constraints derived from the power delivery system's characteristics. This will lead to a more accurate and reliable operation of the power grid, ensuring that the VTs perform their crucial role in monitoring and controlling the system effectively.

7.2.3 Problem Analysis

From the elaborations on the proposed TREE problems, it can be found that these problems are scalable to have a very vast search space, causing the curse of dimensionality. Besides, the TREE problems have multiple complicated constraints, which reduce the size of feasible search space considerably. When the above characteristics of TREE problems are known, some other problem characteristics deserve to be explored, including the relationships among decision variables, objectives, and constraints. After all, an LSMOP can be easily solved by a divide‐and‐conquer method if its decision variables are fully separable. By contrast, when the decision variables have intricate interactions, the difficulty of the problem usually increases considerably.

In this section, we explore the relationships among decision variables, objectives, and constraints using three different methods, including the differential grouping method from [17], and the variable interaction analysis methods in multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm with decision variable analysis (MOEA/DVA) [18] and large‐scale multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (LMEA) [19]. For these analyses, is set to 200 for each problem, and the number of decision variables is 600, 600, 1200, 1200, 1200, and 2400 for TREE1 through TREE6, respectively.

Table 7.2 presents the numbers of interacting and independent decision variables associated with each objective/constraint for each TREE problem. It can be seen that the first objectives of TREE1 through TREE5 are fully separable, while the second ones can be partially divided into three equal‐sized groups without any separable variables. Additionally, all constraints of TREE1 through TREE5, except for TREE6, are fully nonseparable. In summary, the proposed test suite encompasses both separable and nonseparable components.

Table 7.3 presents the numbers of different types of decision variables obtained by MOEA/DVA and LMEA. The analysis results indicate that almost all decision variables of TREE1 through TREE5 are position variables, and approximately half of the decision variables of TREE6 are distance variables concerning relationships between decision variables and objectives. However, significant differences arise when applying MOEA/DVA and LMEA methods to analyze relationships between decision variables and constraints. This discrepancy can be attributed to the fact that both methods were designed for analyzing relationships between decision variables and objectives and might not perform effectively when handling constraints.

7.3 Problem Knowledge‐Driven Coevolutionary Algorithm for Time‐Varying Ratio Error Estimation

Based on the problem analysis as above, it can be noted that the TREE problems pose stiff challenges to the existing MOEAs tailored for general LSMOPs. However, this does not mean that evolutionary algorithms cannot effectively address the TREE problems. For this specific problem, as indicated in previous work, it may be very useful to utilize the information of the problem in designing effective MOEAs. For this reason, the following observation can be found. Despite that the TREE problems are characterized by the vast search space, complicated constraints, and intricate decision variable interactions, another important characteristic of TREE problems is that most VTs work under normal operating conditions, which means that there only exist a small proportion of VTs having relatively large errors. Therefore, it can be inferred that most decision variables in each TREE problem have similar values, which inspires us to exploit this problem knowledge to design a novel search strategy, thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency for solving the challenging TREE problems.

7.3.1 Problem Knowledge Utilization

When we exploit the problem knowledge (i.e., most decision variables in each TREE problem have similar values) to improve the search efficiency of evolutionary algorithms in solving TREE problems, the idea is to coevolve two populations, where one population consists of non‐sparse solutions and the other population is composed of sparse solutions. As shown in Fig. 7.3, when a sparse solution and a non‐sparse solution are selected as parent solutions for offspring generation, most decision variables in the generated offspring solution have similar values, which enables the Pareto optimal solution sets of TREE problems to be handled effectively. Thus, in the case that many algorithms can be used to evolve the population that contains non‐sparse solutions, the main task of solving TREE problems changes to design a novel search strategy to evolve the population that contains sparse solutions.

As introduced in Chapter 4, in recent years, a lot of works have been reported for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. Considering that the search space of TREE problems is more complicated, in this section, we propose a new operator to improve the efficiency in generating sparse solutions. In the operator, decision variables are first divided into multiple groups. Then, a group of decision variables are selected randomly to perform grouped and linked polynomial mutation [20], which has been verified to be effective to generate sparse solutions in SparseEA2 [21]. However, in the grouped and linked polynomial mutation, the direction of mutation is determined randomly, which is prone to mutate a decision variable from zero to nonzero, thus affecting the efficiency of generating sparse solutions. To address this issue, in the proposed operator, a unidirectional mutation operator is incorporated, which always mutates decision variables along the direction of coming close to zero. In this way, the effectiveness and efficiency of generating sparse solutions can be improved greatly. In Fig. 7.4, two illustrative examples are presented, which show that promising sparse solutions can be obtained by performing the proposed unidirectional mutation operator.

To describe the proposed operator in more detail, its pseudocode is presented in Algorithm 7.1. To begin with, the mutation operator divides decision variables into groups by the grouping method . Then, a group of decision variables are selected randomly to perform mutation operator. Specifically, a rand number is first generated and compared with 0.5. If is smaller than 0.5, the unidirectional mutation is performed; otherwise, the bidirectional mutation (i.e., grouped and linked polynomial mutation) is performed. In the unidirectional mutation, the direction of mutation is determined in the following way. Decision variables in the selected decision variable group are first sorted. Then, the decision variable with the median value is selected and termed as . If is larger than zero, which means that at least a half of decision variables in have values larger than zero, all decision variables in are mutated along the direction of decreasing their values to zero. Otherwise, there exist at least a half decision variables in that their values are smaller than zero; thus, all decision variables in are mutated along the direction of increasing their values to zero.

7.3.2 Framework of PKCEA

This section gives the framework of the proposed problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm, namely, PKCEA. As shown in Fig. 7.5, the proposed algorithm contains two optimization tasks, namely, the main optimization task and the auxiliary optimization task. The main optimization task is addressed by population , which uses the conventional genetic operators (i.e., simulated binary crossover [22] and polynomial mutation [23]) to generate offspring solutions. The auxiliary optimization task is addressed by population , which uses the improved grouped and linked polynomial mutation operator to generate offspring solutions. In fact, a lot of similar frameworks [24–27] have been reported in recent years, which demonstrate their effectiveness to solve multi‐objective optimization problems with constraints by introducing auxiliary optimization. However, the majority of existing algorithms devote their efforts to solving medium and small‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems, and the auxiliary optimization is designed by easing the difficulty brought by constraints [28], thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency of environmental selection. By contrast, the algorithm PKCEA is proposed to solve LSMOPs and the auxiliary optimization is designed by focusing on generating sparse solutions, which enables the generated solutions similar to the Pareto optimal solution sets as much as possible, thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency in solving TREE problems.

Algorithm 7.2 gives the detailed procedure of PKCEA. To begin with, two initial populations and are generated, where population is generated by the random method and population is generated by Algorithm 4.1. When solutions in the two populations are evaluated, the algorithm enters the loop. In the loop, first, two mating parent pools, namely, and , are obtained by the binary tournament selection method, where the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of solutions are used as the selection criteria. Then, two offspring populations are generated by genetic operators. Specially, the offspring in are generated by the simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation operators, the offspring in are generated by the improved grouped and linked polynomial mutation operator. Next, the two offspring populations are combined with and to obtain populations and . Finally, when the solutions in and are evaluated, the environmental selection strategy of non‐dominated sorting based genetic algorithm‐II (NSGA‐II) [29] is performed to update populations and . The loop iterates until the number of function evaluations is not smaller than the maximum number of function evaluations , and the algorithm terminates and outputs population .

7.3.3 Experimental Comparisons

In this section, experimental comparisons between the proposed algorithm and several representative MOEAs are performed on the formulated TREE test problems, namely, TREE1–TREE5. For each test problem, the number of decision variables is set to 3000, 6000, 9000, 12,000, and 15,000; thus, there are totally 25 test instances used for performance assessment. The proposed algorithm is compared with five MOEAs, including NSGA‐II [29], large‐scale multi‐objective optimization framework (LSMOF) [30], large‐scale multi‐objective competitive swarm optimizer (LMOCSO) [31], constrained large‐scale reference vector guided evolutionary algorithm (CLS‐RVEA) [32], and FLEA [33].

In the experiments, the maximum number of function evaluations is adopted as the termination criterion, which is set to for each algorithm on each test problem with denoting the number of decision variables. For all algorithms, the population size is set to 100. For the proposed PKCEA, the ordered grouping method is used, and the number of decision variable groups is set to four. For the compared algorithms, their algorithm‐specific parameters are set to the values in their original papers. Considering that the Pareto fronts of the TREE problems are unknown, the hypervolume (HV) [34] indicator is used for performance assessment. It is worth noting that the experiments as mentioned above are performed on PlatEMO [35].

Table 7.4 shows the HV results obtained by the six algorithms on the 25 test instances. From the table, it can be seen that the proposed algorithm PKCEA achieves the best overall performance, having obtained the best result on most test instances. LSMOF and FLEA show inferior overall performance than the proposed PKCEA, but they can always obtain a nonzero HV value on each test instance. By contrast, the HV values obtained by the other three algorithms on some test instances are zero, due to the fact that they fail to obtain any feasible solution. To be specific, NSGA‐II fails to obtain any feasible solution on the TREE3, TREE4, TREE5, high‐dimensional TREE1, and high‐dimensional TREE2 problems, LMOCSO cannot obtain any feasible solution on the TREE3 and TREE4 problems, and CLS‐RVEA does not obtain any feasible solution on TREE3.

Figure 7.6 plots the populations and convergence curves with median HV values obtained by the six algorithms on the TREE1, TREE3, and TREE5 problems with 3000 decision variables. It is worth noting that the populations and convergence curves of NSGA‐II, LMOCSO, and CLS‐RVEA on some problems are not provided since they fail to converge to feasible regions. From the figure, it can be seen that the proposed algorithm exhibits better performance.

7.4 Summary

In this chapter, a data‐driven problem formulation method is proposed for ratio error estimation of VTs, which offers several advantages, including lower cost compared to on‐site/off‐line calibration, real‐time estimation for early warnings of potential faulty VTs, and versatility in handling different substation types and VT models. These advantages make the method practical and valuable for real‐world applications. Based on the data‐driven problem formulation method, a number of test problems are proposed. In the proposed TREE problems, a lot of challenges are associated, including the vast search space, the complex constraints, and the intricate interactions between decision variables.

To solve the challenging TREE problems, a problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm is reported, which introduces a sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization as the auxiliary optimization. In the auxiliary optimization, a novel genetic operator is proposed to improve the efficiency of generating sparse solutions, thus enabling the Pareto optimal solution sets of TREE problems to be solved effectively. Experimental studies show that the proposed algorithm is superior over the compared MOEAs.

8
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Radiotherapy Planning

8.1 Introduction

Since X‐ray was found by Röntgen in the 1890s, ionizing radiation has received increasing attention in the therapy of malignant tumors. With the invention of linear accelerators in the 1950s, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging in the 1970s, and multileaf collimators (MLCs) in the 1980s, radiotherapy has become an important modality used in cancer treatment. Together with surgery and chemotherapy, nearly 70% cancer patients have received radiotherapy during their course of illness [1]. To provide conformal dose distribution for different clinical cases, intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) has served as an effective technique for radiotherapy, able to generate individual‐specific therapeutic fields by adjusting the angles, intensities, and shapes of radiation [2].

8.1.1 Challenges of IMRT Planning

As illustrated in Fig. 8.1, the therapeutic fields are formed by the photons or protons transmitted through a MLC, where the photons or protons are emitted by radiation beams produced by a linear accelerator [3]. The therapeutic fields form heterogeneous dose distribution, so as to meet the clinical requirements of a given cancer case, i.e., maximizing the tumor control probability while minimizing the normal tissue complication probability [4]. Therefore, the core issue of IMRT planning is essentially an optimization problem, where the decision variables include the angles, intensities, and shapes of radiation, and the objectives include the satisfaction of the dose distribution in the planning tumor volume (PTV consisting of tumor cells) and the minimization of the dose distribution in the organ at risk (OAR consisting of healthy cells).

IMRT planning introduces challenging optimization problems characterized by discrete variables, high‐dimensional decision spaces, many objectives, and computationally expensive functions. First, the therapeutic fields are partitioned into many small grids to ease the calculation of dose distribution; hence, their shapes are determined by integer variables rather than continuous variables. Second, since all the small grids can only have the same intensity at a time, many apertures with different shapes and intensities are required to form a therapeutic field with heterogeneous dose distribution, which leads to thousands of shape‐related variables. Third, a clinical case usually has multiple PTV and OAR regions and each region corresponds to multiple clinical requirements, which leads to dozens of conflicting objectives to be optimized simultaneously. Lastly, the calculation of dose distribution involves the multiplication of large matrices, where too many function evaluations are unaffordable in clinical practice. Due to these difficulties of IMRT planning, a variety of methods have been developed in the last three decades, and some of which are introduced in the following.

8.1.2 IMRT Planning Methods

Existing IMRT planning methods can be roughly grouped into two categories, including two‐step optimization methods and direct aperture optimization methods. The two‐step optimization methods aim to obtain the optimal dose distribution and then obtain the corresponding apertures, where the first step is known as fluence map optimization and the second step is known as MLC sequencing. The task of fluence map optimization is to obtain the optimal intensity for each small grid in the therapeutic fields, and thus the therapeutic fields can form heterogeneous dose distribution in the PTV and OAR regions. Fluence map optimization is a continuous optimization problem that has been handled by various advanced techniques, including analytical algorithms (e.g., Fourier transform [5] and Taylor series expansion [6]), mathematical programming (e.g., mixed integer programming [7] and quadratic programming [8]), machine learning (e.g., regression forests [9] and deep neural networks [10]), and metaheuristics (e.g., simulated annealing [11] and genetic algorithms [12]). While the small grids with different intensities cannot be implemented directly, the task of MLC sequencing is to obtain the optimal apertures, where the small grids in each aperture share the same intensity. Thus, MLC sequencing aims to minimize the difference between the fluence map and the superposition of all apertures, which is usually handled by column generation methods [13, 14].

The direct aperture optimization methods aim to obtain the optimal apertures directly, so as to eliminate the distortion of intensities caused by MLC sequencing. Obviously, direct aperture optimization is more challenging, since it is a combinatorial optimization problem. Some methods have been suggested for direct aperture optimization, such as enumeration [15], gradient descent [16], random search [17], local search [18], and genetic algorithms [19]. Nevertheless, direct aperture optimization is so complex that it cannot be solved in a totally black‐box manner, where problem‐dependent search strategies are required to avoid invalid solutions brought by the physical limitations of MLC.

The difficulty encountered by the above methods mainly lies in the balance between many conflicting objectives (i.e., clinical requirements). Basically, larger intensities are more effective for killing tumor cells but also damage more healthy cells [20]. Therefore, MOEAs have been suggested for IMRT planning in recent research [21, 22], which can provide many candidate solutions with diverse trade‐offs between objectives, thus highly reducing the human expertise required by medical physicists. Nevertheless, IMRT planning involves a large number of discrete variables, where MOEAs should be equipped with customized search strategies for high efficiency [23, 24].

8.2 Problem Formulation

IMRT planning is essentially a combinatorial LSMOP, which aims to find the optimal angles, intensities, and shapes of multiple apertures for meeting many clinical requirements of a given cancer case. The clinical requirements are related to the dose distribution determined by apertures, where the apertures are two‐dimensional regions partitioned into many small grids and the dose distribution corresponds to a three‐dimensional region partitioned into many voxels (i.e., small cubes). Here, the angles of apertures are fixed by experience while the intensities and shapes of apertures are optimized by optimizers, and thus the dose deposition coefficient of the th voxel in terms of the th small grid can be calculated by Monte Carlo methods [25] in advance. Although there have been many generic MOEAs tailored for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, they are ineffective for solving the problem defined in Eq. (8.6) due to two main reasons. First, most generic MOEAs evolve populations in continuous decision spaces, where the search strategies (e.g., decision variable grouping and decision space reduction) cannot handle the discrete variables related to aperture shapes. Second, many solutions generated in a stochastic search paradigm are likely to be invalid due to the physical limitations of MLC; moreover, the repair of invalid solutions is highly disruptive to the evolution of populations. To address these issues, several MOEAs have been suggested for IMRT planning with customized search strategies in recent years [23, 24], where the first MOEA tailored for IMRT planning is introduced in Section 8.3.

8.3 Bi‐Encoding Coevolutionary Algorithm for IMRT Planning

The multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm for intensity‐modulated radiotherapy planning (MOEA/IMRT) suggests a bi‐encoding coevolutionary framework for solving the problem defined in Eq. (8.6) [24]. More specifically, one population represented in fine encoding is evolved for the local exploitation of complex and irregular aperture shapes, and another population represented in rough encoding is evolved for the global exploration of simple and regular aperture shapes. The population represented in fine encoding serves as the final output, which provides diverse candidate treatment plans for medical physicists and doctors. On the other hand, the population represented in rough encoding forms a low‐dimensional decision space for the acceleration of the convergence of the population represented in fine encoding, where the transfer of useful genetic material has been verified to be effective in handling complex constraints [29]. Furthermore, MOEA/IMRT customizes two local search strategies for repairing invalid solutions and accelerating the convergence, respectively.

8.3.1 Bi‐Encoding Scheme of MOEA/IMRT

While the intensities of apertures can be directly represented by real variables, the first issue that should be addressed is to represent the shapes of apertures by proper variables. Intuitively, as shown in Fig. 8.2, a binary matrix can be associated with an aperture to indicate whether each small grid is shielded or not. However, most solutions represented by this encoding scheme will violate the physical limitations of MLC shown in Fig. 8.1, as the unshielded small grids must be successive in each row. Therefore, the fine encoding scheme of MOEA/IMRT uses many integer variables to represent the positions of MLC leaves for each aperture, and the rough encoding scheme of MOEA/IMRT uses four integer variables to determine a rectangular region of unshielded small grids.

Figure 8.3 illustrates the bi‐encoding scheme used in MOEA/IMRT. For an IMRT task with radiation beams and apertures for each beam, a solution is the concatenation of vectors, where vector encodes the intensity and shape of the th aperture. To be specific, for an aperture represented in fine encoding, it consists of decision variables with denoting the number of rows of the aperture, where the integer denotes the position of the th left leaf of the MLC, the integer denotes the position of the th right leaf of the MLC, and . Besides, the real number denotes the intensity of the aperture. For an aperture represented in rough encoding, it consists of five decision variables, where the real number denotes the intensity of the aperture and the integers , , , and denote the horizontal position of the upper left corner, the vertical position of the upper left corner, the width, and the height of the rectangular region of unshielded small grids, respectively. In short, a solution represented in fine encoding contains variables forming a high‐dimensional decision space, and a solution represented in rough encoding contains variables forming a low‐dimensional decision space.

As can be observed from Fig. 8.3, the solutions represented in fine encoding can search for irregular apertures to be used in clinical practice, while the solutions represented in rough encoding can only search for rectangular apertures to assist the optimization of the solutions represented in fine encoding. Thus, the exploitation and exploration can be balanced by the cooperation of the two encoding schemes. In order to transfer useful genetic material between the solutions represented in different encoding schemes, MOEA/IMRT suggests the conversion strategies presented in Fig. 8.4. 8.3.2 Local Search Strategies of MOEA/IMRT

The two encoding schemes consider the physical nature of MLC leaves, but they are still unable to prevent invalid apertures such as those with very small shapes or disconnected shapes. Besides, the co‐evolution of two populations with different encoding schemes is not efficient enough to converge in the high‐dimensional decision space. To handle these problems, MOEA/IMRT develops a local search strategy for repairing invalid solutions and a local search strategy for finding better solutions.

As illustrated in Fig. 8.5, an aperture represented in fine encoding may be too small (i.e., the number of unshielded grids is less than a threshold) or disconnected (i.e., some of the unshielded grids are not connected), and an aperture represented in rough encoding may also be too small. To repair such apertures, a local search strategy is developed in MOEA/IMRT for ensuring clinical practicality. Considering a population represented in fine encoding and a population represented in rough encoding, Algorithm 8.2 elaborates on the procedure of repairing invalid solutions in the two populations. For each solution represented in fine encoding (Line 1), each of its apertures is repaired by Eq. (8.9) (Lines 2 and 3). While for each solution represented in rough encoding (Line 4), each of its apertures is repaired by Eq. (8.10) (Lines 5 and 6). Lastly, the repaired populations are directly returned (Line 7).

The aforementioned bi‐encoding scheme and repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT focus on the optimization of aperture shapes. To further improve the convergence speed, the second local search strategy of MOEA/IMRT aims to enhance the optimization of aperture intensities, whose procedure is described in Algorithm 8.3. Given a population represented in fine encoding, the non‐dominated solutions in are firstly copied to a new set (Line 1), whose shape‐related variables are retained while intensity‐related variables are to be optimized. Then, a new population with solutions having only aperture intensities is randomly initialized (Line 2), i.e., each solution has only one real variable. To evaluate on the objectives of IMRT planning, each solution in is associated with a solution randomly selected from (Line 3). In other words, the decision vector to be evaluated consists of the shape‐related variables of a solution from and the intensity‐related variable of each solution in , and thus the aperture shapes are retained in and the aperture intensities are optimized by evolving . The evolution of is conducted for a predefined number of generations, by means of the mating selection strategy (Line 6), variation operators (Line 7), and environmental selection strategy (Line 9) of MOEA/IMRT, whose procedures are elaborated in Section 8.3.3. It should be noted that the optimization of aperture intensities consumes additional function evaluations, hence it is just conducted with a population size and 100 generations after every 100 main generations of MOEA/IMRT. This way, the local search does not deteriorate the efficiency of the whole algorithm obviously.

8.3.3 Procedure of MOEA/IMRT

With the bi‐encoding scheme and two local search strategies, the procedure of MOEA/IMRT is described in Algorithm 8.4. First, a population with solutions represented in fine encoding is randomly initialized (Line 1), and a population with solutions represented in rough encoding is randomly initialized (Line 2). Then, the solutions in the two populations are repaired by the repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 3), and the fitness values of all the solutions are calculated to be used in selection strategies (Lines 4 and 5). MOEA/IMRT adopts the fitness assignment strategy of SPEA2 with shift‐based density estimation [30] as described in Algorithm 8.5, which is the same as that of the original SPEA2 [31] except for a new method to measure the distances between solutions. When calculating the Euclidean distances to a solution in the objective space, all the objective values of the other solutions are shifted to be not less than the objective values of (Line 7 of Algorithm 8.5). Such a shift‐based density estimation can consider both the convergence and diversity of solutions in the Euclidean distances, which is particularly effective for many‐objective optimization problems including IMRT planning where general selection strategies suffer from the Pareto dominance resistance phenomenon [32].

 

At each generation, the mating pool is constructed by selecting parents from the population via binary tournament selection according to the fitness of solutions (Line 7). Then, offspring solutions are generated by simulated binary crossover [33] and polynomial mutation [34] (Line 8), and the first decision variables of each offspring solution are rounded since these shape‐related variables can only be integers (Lines 9–12). Similarly, the mating pool is constructed by selecting parents from the population via binary tournament selection according to the fitness of solutions (Line 13). Then, offspring solutions are generated (Line 14) and the first four decision variables of each offspring solution are rounded since these shape‐related variables can only be integers (Lines 15–18). Afterward, the offspring solutions represented in two encoding schemes are repaired by the repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 19) and transferred by the conversion strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 20). After combing each of and with the offspring solutions represented in the same encoding scheme, and are truncated by the environmental selection strategy of SPEA2 with shift‐based density estimation (Lines 21 and 22). As presented in Algorithm 8.6, the procedure of environmental selection is the same as that of the original SPEA2 except for the shift‐based density estimation‐based Euclidean distance calculation. Lastly, the local search strategy for intensity optimization is conducted periodically to further enhance the convergence of (Lines 23–25), and is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 26).

At each generation of MOEA/IMRT, the time complexity is for mating pool selection, for offspring generation, for offspring repair, for offspring evaluation, for offspring conversion, and for environmental selection, where denotes the number of decision variables, denotes the number of objectives, denotes the number of voxels in a region, denotes the number of small grids in a therapeutic field, denotes the number of radiation beams, and denotes the number of apertures. Besides, the time complexity of the local search strategy for intensity optimization is with being the number of generations for intensity optimization, but it is not included in the total time complexity since it is rarely conducted. As a result, the time complexity of one generation of MOEA/IMRT is , which is mainly determined by the scales of dose distribution regions and apertures of IMRT planning tasks.

8.4 Experimental Studies

To study the performance of MOEA/IMRT, it is compared with several representative IMRT methods and MOEAs on a number of clinical cases. The compared methods include Shepard's method [17], NSGA‐II [35], CCGDE3 [36], LSMOF‐NSGA‐II [37], LMOCSO [38], and MOEA/IMRT, where Shepard's method is the first direct aperture optimization method based on simulated annealing and mathematical programming, NSGA‐II is a classical MOEA, CCGDE3 is a decision variable grouping‐based MOEA, LSMOF‐NSGA‐II is a decision space reduction‐based MOEA, and LMOCSO is a novel search strategy‐based MOEA. The population size is set to 100, the number of function evaluations is set to 100,000, and the number of transferred solutions in MOEA/IMRT is set to 10. For Shepard's method generating a single solution in one run, it is executed for 100 independent runs with 100 uniformly distributed weight vectors for aggregating all the objectives, and the number of function evaluations is also equally divided. For NSGA‐II, CCGDE3, LSMOF‐NSGA‐II, and LMOCSO, they represent solutions by using the fine encoding scheme given in Fig. 8.3 and repair invalid solutions by using the local search strategy given in Algorithm 8.2. Five clinical cases are taken from the real world, whose statistics are listed in Table 8.1. It can be found that the number of objectives varies from 9 to 25 and the number of decision variables varies from 1950 to 2715, which results in typical combinatorial LSMOPs. The populations obtained by the methods are assessed by HV [39] since the true Pareto fronts are unknown.

Table 8.2 lists the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold. It can be found from the table that Shepard's method obtains the worst performance since it generates only a single solution in one run and cannot maintain a good diversity for the solutions obtained in different runs. NSGA‐II obtains the second worst performance among the six compared methods, since it does not contain any strategy for searching in high‐dimensional decision spaces. By contrast, the three large‐scale MOEAs exhibit significantly better performance, and the LMOCSO based on a novel competitive swarm optimizer seems very suitable for IMRT planning tasks. Nevertheless, they are underperformed by the customized method MOEA/IMRT, which suggests a bi‐encoding scheme and two local search strategies leading to the best performance on all the cases.

For a visual comparison, Fig. 8.6 plots the dose–volume histograms of the treatment plans obtained by six methods on the Sneezer case, which is a popular visualization method for physicists. A dose–volume histogram contains several curves representing the cumulative doses in each region, where a point on a curve indicates that the proportion of voxels with doses larger than is . Figure 8.6 plots the curves of three regions (i.e., PTV, OAR1, and OAR2) of the treatment plan having the minimum sum of all objectives in the population with the median HV value obtained by each method and also plots the vertical lines of maximum dose of PTV, minimum dose of PTV, maximum dose of OAR1, and maximum dose of OAR2. Ideally, the curves should decrease sharply, and the vertical parts of the curves should be to the left of the lines of maximum doses and to the right of the lines of minimum doses. As can be observed from the figure, the vertical parts of the curves of PTV obtained by Shepard's method, NSGA‐II, CCGDE3, and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II are mostly to the left of the line of minimum dose of PTV, which means that the obtained treatment plans are ineffective to kill tumor cells. By contrast, the vertical parts of the curves of PTV obtained by LMOCSO and MOEA/IMRT are mostly in between the lines of minimum dose and maximum dose of PTV, which means that the obtained treatment plans are obviously more effective. In particular, the curve of PTV obtained by MOEA/IMRT decreases more sharply than that obtained by LMOCSO, which further evidences the superiority of customized search strategies over generic large‐scale MOEAs for IMRT planning.

8.5 Summary

This chapter introduces an emerging application of evolutionary large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, namely, IMRT planning. The challenges of this task lie in a large number of discrete variables and dozens of objectives, and the strict limitations of MLC also lead to many invalid solutions. Mathematical programming methods [7, 16], heuristics [6, 15], and deep learning methods [10, 40] are incapable of handling the conflicting objectives for providing diverse treatment plans, while general evolutionary algorithms [12, 22] are ineffective to optimize the large number of variables within a limited number of function evaluations. Therefore, several MOEAs have been developed for IMRT planning with customized search strategies [23, 24], such as the bi‐encoding scheme and local search strategies of MOEA/IMRT. We can conclude from the experimental results that large‐scale MOEAs are indeed more effective than conventional optimizers including general MOEAs for IMRT planning. However, the research of evolutionary multi‐objective optimization mostly focuses on continuous optimization, while MOEA/IMRT can further improve the performance on IMRT planning by developing customized search strategies for combinatorial optimization.

9
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Deep Learning

9.1 Introduction

Deep learning has made significant success in tackling various machine learning tasks, including image processing and computer vision [1], natural language processing [2], and object detection [3]. To achieve desirable performance, it is widely recognized that the weights and architecture of deep neural networks (DNNs) are very crucial. Hence, optimizing the weights and designing the architectures of DNNs remain a hot research field in recent years.

Regarding optimizing weights of DNNs, a number of learning algorithms have been developed, including the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [4], RMSProp [5], and Adam [6], among several others, most of which are gradient‐based methods. The success of DNNs has proven that gradient‐based methods are efficient in training DNNs due to the rapid convergence speed provided by the gradient information. But, they also suffer from several limitations [7–11]. First, they may easily get trapped into local optimums or saddle points due to their greedy nature [7, 8]. Second, a regularization term usually needs to be included to alleviate overfitting [12], which may not always lead to the desired training performance, since it is nontrivial to specify the hyperparameter for regularization. Finally, a number of other hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, momentum, and drop rate, must be carefully predefined [11].

Regarding designing architectures of DNNs, early efforts are devoted to manually designing various neural architectures. Examples of this category include the ResNet [13], DenseNet [14], and GoogLeNet [15, 16]. Due to the requirements of human domain knowledge and expertise in handcrafted neural architectures, a hot research direction called neural architecture search (NAS) has arisen since it first appeared in [17]. To solve the NAS task, a variety of optimization techniques have been adopted for NAS to yield high‐performance architectures, including reinforcement learning (RL) [18, 19], gradient optimization [20, 21], Bayesian optimization [22], and others [23].

As a class of population‐based meta‐heuristics, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been shown effective in solving the weight optimization of neural networks (NNs) (i.e., the training of NNs) and the architecture search of DNNs (i.e., NAS). Compared to gradient‐based approaches to training NNs and other optimization approaches to NAS, EAs are more insensitive to local optimums due to the attractive exploratory ability [11] and perform better in handling multiple objectives without extra hyperparameters [24], which can provide a set of potential solutions for decision. Nevertheless, it is still difficult for EAs to solve large‐scale optimization problems for DNNs (e.g., training DNNs) [11], since EAs suffer from poor scalability to the search dimension; besides, it is also challenging for EAs to solve the NAS task, because equipping EAs with an effective encoding scheme and genetic operators for NAS are not easily attainable, where the population characteristics of EAs further makes NAS need more computational resources. This motivates many researchers to improve EAs for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems in deep learning and this chapter presents two state‐of‐the‐art EAs for two typical multi‐objective optimization problems for deep learning: a gradient‐guided multi‐objective EA for training DNNs (termed GEMONN) and an action command‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA for searching neural architectures of DNNs (termed ACEncoding).

9.2 Gradient‐Guided Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Training Deep Neural Networks

To obtain better weights for NNs, many EAs have been suggested for training NNs [10, 11,25–31]. For instance, Whitley et al. [27] adopted a genetic algorithm to optimize the weights of NNs, where experimental results demonstrated its competitiveness on training NNs. Montana and Davis [26] trained a feedforward NNs with a total of 126 weights via a tailored genetic algorithm, which was shown to outperform gradient‐based approaches. Despite their superiority in training NNs, EAs are less efficient in solving the training of DNNs due to the curse of dimensionality [32]. To address this issue, some attempts have been made to enhance the scalability of EAs in training large‐scale NNs, especially DNNs. For example, Gong et al. [31] suggested a bi‐objective EA to optimize the weights of sparse DNNs by only considering the biases instead of all weights, mainly because the biases are the main factor for controlling the sparsity of hidden layers; Liu et al. [10] suggested an evolutionary layer‐wise structure learning approach for optimizing network weights, which reduces the large search space by limiting the weight value to 0 or 1 and making multiple weights in the same region share the same value; Sun et al. [11] developed a single‐objective EA to optimize the weights of DNNs, where the weight optimization was converted into the optimization of orthogonal bias vector in weight space; instead of simplifying the optimization problem, Such et al. [33] used the parallel computing devices to enhance the search ability, aiming to improve the scalability of EAs in optimizing the weights of DNNs, by which millions of weights can be effectively optimized on a single modern desktop; Cui et al. [8] proposed an evolutionary approach to optimize the weights by combining the SGD and an EA, where the EA enhances the stability of the SGD and guarantees steady reduction of loss function. Most of these evolutionary approaches for training large‐scale NNs aim to address the curse of dimensionality by reducing the search space (i.e., number of weights to be optimized), which may miss the optimal search region and increase the probability of getting trapped in local optima [34].

To remedy this limitation, this section introduces a gradient‐guided evolutionary approach to training DNNs (called GEMONN), which can take advantages of the strength of both gradient descent (GD) and EAs. The presented crossover is a gradient‐guided simulated binary crossover operator [35], termed gSBX, for optimizing the weights of DNNs. The search direction of gSBX is defined to be the same as the gradient of the parent to strike a balance between exploitation and exploration in optimizing the weights of DNNs. gSBX is then embedded in an evolutionary multi‐objective algorithm to train DNNs, which minimizes the training loss and the network sparsity at the same time. To validate the performance of the proposed approach, GEMONN is adopted to train the weights of four types of NNs, namely, auto‐encoder (AE), stacked auto‐encoder (SAE), long short‐term memory (LSTM), and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Experimental results indicate that GEMONN is able to enhance the scalability of EAs in training large‐scale neural networks having up to millions of weights.

In the following, we first present the formal definition of neural network training, then the GEMONN for training the DNNs is elaborated. Finally, experimental comparisons between the GEMONN and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for network training are showcased and discussed.

9.2.2 Gradient‐Guided Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Training of Deep Neural Networks

9.2.2.1 Motivations

In spite of the promising performance of existing evolutionary approaches to training NNs, most of them encounter difficulties in optimizing a large number of weights in DNNs [11]. The limitation of these approaches can mainly be attributed to the dimension reduction strategies they employ, which typically can address the curse of dimensionality to some extent but is easily vulnerable to get trapped in local optima [34]. Hence, these approaches have to reduce the number of optimized weights due to the limitation of the search ability of EAs for large‐scale optimization [32]. Besides, there are some approaches [8, 31] directly combining EAs and the GD to conduct search in the original search space, where the weights are successively updated by a traditional genetic operator and GD. However, the poor scalability of EAs to large‐scale optimization problems is also not overcame. In other words, the EA in these approaches can only guarantee that the best fitness in the population does not degrade, while the GD is mainly responsible for finding better solutions in the original search space.

To better understanding the limitation of traditional genetic operators, Fig. 9.1 illustrates the difference between the search behaviors of genetic operators and GD in optimizing a multimodal function . More specifically, the popular genetic operator simulated binary crossover (SBX) [35] is taken as an example in Fig. 9.1(a), where the generated offspring solutions distribute on both sides of the parent , since SBX determines the search direction randomly and enables more unknown areas to be explored. In other words, SBX makes many unnecessary search efforts, which becomes even more serious in optimizing the weights of DNNs in a high‐dimensional search space. The GD method, by contrast, has shown better exploitation ability since the search direction is always opposite to the gradient of , as shown in Fig. 9.1(b). However, an unsuitable step size (determined by the learning rate) is likely to drive to a local optimum.

As illustrated in Fig. 9.1(c), the weakness of SBX, i.e., it generates offspring solutions only in the expected direction, can be remedied by the GD. Vice versa, the vulnerability of the gradient approach to local optimums can be alleviated by the genetic operator. To be more specific, the introduction of gradient information into the genetic operator can guide the search behavior toward promising directions, thereby significantly enhancing the search efficiency. Meanwhile, the generation of multiple offspring solutions can considerably reduce the probability of getting trapped into local optima and improve the exploration ability of the GD. In addition, this combination also eliminates the use of learning rate, which is difficult to be predefined or adapted.

Following the above basic idea, a gradient‐guided evolutionary search approach to training DNNs will be presented below. In contrast to existing approaches that are usually tailored for a specific type of DNN, the proposed generic approach is applicable to different types of DNNs.

Among these crossovers, SBX exhibits better performance on most test problems as demonstrated in [42]. 9.2.2.5 Sparsity in gSBX

To maintain the sparsity of the offspring solutions in gSBX, it is intuitive to make the offspring solutions have the same or a higher degree of sparsity than their parents. For this purpose, gSBX sets each decision variable of an offspring solution to zero if the variable of the corresponding parent is zero. Thus, the number of zero weights in the offspring solution is always equal to or larger than the number of zero weights in the parent. According to (9.5), holds if we set . 9.2.2.6 Procedure of gSBX

The main steps of gSBX are listed in Algorithm 9.1. It can be seen from the algorithm that two parents, and , are randomly selected from population , which are used to generate two offspring solutions and . For each dimension, , , , , , and are determined in sequence, and the decision variables and are calculated accordingly. A preliminary comparative study is performed to verify the advantage of the proposed gSBX over original SBX. In the comparison, both gSBX and SBX are implemented in a simple genetic algorithm to minimize the following function:

(9.15)

where . The population size is set to 100 and the number of generations is 100. Besides, the GD with a learning rate of 0.1 is also adopted to minimize the function for 10,000 epochs. The minimum objective values found by the steepest descent method, genetic algorithm with SBX, and genetic algorithm with the proposed gSBX are plotted in Fig. 9.4. It can be found that the steepest descent method quickly gets stuck a local optimum, while SBX is able to find an acceptable solution, although it converges slower than the steepest descent method. The proposed gSBX has a similar convergence speed to the gradient method, and finds a similar objective value to SBX. From these results, we can conclude that gSBX can strike a balance between exploitation and exploration. Therefore, it is expected to be efficient in training DNNs with a large number of weights.

Based on the proposed gSBX, a gradient‐guided evolutionary approach is proposed to train DNNs, the details of which are presented in the next subsection.

9.2.3 Framework of GEMONN

Algorithm 9.2 presents the procedure of the proposed GEMONN. To begin with, a population with predefined size is initialized, where the decision variables (i.e., weights) of each solution are set to a random value within or 0 with the same probability. Then, the objective values of each solution are evaluated and the gradient in terms of the training loss is calculated. In each generation of GEMONN, a number of solutions is selected from the population by the mating selection strategy of NSGA‐II [44] and used to generate the same number of offspring solutions by the proposed gSBX. Then, the offspring population is combined with the parent population, and half the solutions in the combined population are retained for the next generation by the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II. After the evolution terminates, a single solution should be picked up from the final population as the output. For this purpose, strategies for updating Pareto optimal solutions and for selecting a final solution are developed.

A flowchart of the proposed GEMONN is plotted in Fig. 9.5. In the following, the details of the main components of GEMONN, including solution evaluation, Pareto optimal solution update, and final solution selection, are described separately.

9.2.3.1 Quality Evaluation

Given a training set and a DNN , the proposed GEMONN calculates the following two objective values for each solution :

(9.16)

where the decision vector denotes the set of all the weights in , and is the output of with the weights being . The first objective indicates the complexity of the DNN, where a smaller means to a sparser network. Here, the ‐norm is adopted to measure the complexity, which is believed to be effective since it directly counts the number of nonzero weights [9, 43]. The second objective indicates the training loss averaged over all the training samples, where the cross entropy loss (CE) [45] is adopted for supervised learning tasks and the mean squared error (MSE) [9] is employed for unsupervised learning tasks. Specifically, is defined as

(9.17)

where denotes the th label of the th sample, denotes the th feature of the th sample, is the total number of labels, and is the total number of features.

Since the network may overfit the training data if only the training loss is minimized, we consider the network complexity to alleviate overfitting. As shown in [9], the two objectives and are conflicting with each other since a network with lower training loss usually corresponds to a higher complexity. Owing to the delicate selection strategy provided by evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, however, a set of solutions striking a good trade‐off between the two objectives can be found, and a network with acceptable training loss without overfitting the training set is expected to be obtained.

9.2.3.2 Update of Pareto Optimal Solutions

Once the evolutionary optimization process is completed, a strategy for updating Pareto optimal solutions is designed for the final exploitation. To be specific, the dominated solutions in the population are removed, and then each non‐dominated solution is fine‐tuned by SGD [46] with a learning rate of 0.1 for one epoch. It is worth noting that only the nonzero weights are updated here, while the zero weights are kept unchanged. Such the proposed trick can decrease the training loss while maintaining the network sparsity, and we call it sparse stochastic gradient descent (SSGD) hereafter.

9.2.3.3 Final Solution Selection

Last but not the least, a single solution should be selected from the fine‐tuned population as the output. Intuitively, it is unreasonable to select the solution with the lowest training loss or complexity, as the former tends to overfit the training set and the latter is usually not well trained. Since the solutions in the knee area of the population have a better trade‐off between the two objectives [9], they are usually preferred in many scenarios [10, 31]. Based on this idea, the proposed GEMONN selects a solution according to the following criteria:

(9.18)

The first criterion aims to find the solutions whose training loss has the same order of magnitude as , where is the solution having the lowest training loss in the population, i.e., . The second criterion also aims to guarantee the training performance of the selected solution. The third criterion is used to find the final solution according to , which calculates the angle between the left and right neighbors of the solution [47].

9.2.3.4 Time Complexity Analysis

 The time complexity of proposed GEMONN is mainly determined by two components, i.e., the calculation of gradients and the optimization process of NSGA‐II. According to [48], the time complexity for calculating the gradients is , where and are the size of a mini‐batch and feature dimensionality, respectively.
