9.2.4 Empirical Studies

9.2.4.1 Neural Networks to be Trained

The performance of the proposed GEMONN is verified on four types of NNs, including AE, SAE [49], LSTM [50], and CNNs [18]. A brief introduction to the training of the four types of NNs is given in the following.

  1. Auto‐encoder (AE). As a fully connected (FC) feedforward NN with a single hidden layer, AE is often used for dimensionality reduction, where the output is expected to be the same as the input and the hidden layer can be regarded as a meaningful and reduced representation of the training sample. As a result, AE can be trained in an unsupervised manner, and many existing EAs have been adopted to train it [10, 11, 31]. To train AE by the proposed GEMONN, the MSE is adopted as the second objective. Besides, the sigmoid activation function is applied in the hidden layer.
  2. Stacked auto‐encoder (SAE). By using AE as the building blocks, SAE can reduce the training sample layer by layer and perform classification at last. With the greedy layer‐wise training process, the dependency of weights in different layers can be properly handled, and the weights in each layer can be optimized separately. The training of SAE consists of two phases [11, 51], i.e., pre‐training and fine‐tuning. The pre‐training phase trains a set of AEs with different numbers of hidden nodes by minimizing the reconstruction error. Then, these AEs are stacked together and tailed by an FC layer, and the fine‐tuning phase optimizes all the weights for minimizing the classification error. To train SAE by the proposed GEMONN, the MSE is adopted as the second objective in the pre‐training phase and the CE is adopted in the fine‐tuning phase.
  3. Long short‐term memory (LSTM). LSTM is currently one of the most popular recurrent NNs for many deep‐learning tasks, in which the connections between layers are much more complex than those in feedforward NNs. Since all the weights in LSTM should be optimized together, it is much more difficult than training SAE whose weights are optimized layer by layer, and none of the existing evolutionary approaches have been applied to it. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed genetic operator in training DNNs without dimensionality reduction, we also use the proposed GEMONN to train LSTM with its structure shown in Fig. 9.6(a), where the CE is adopted as the second objective.
  4. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs). CNNs are also powerful NNs for many deep learning tasks, especially computer vision. To investigate the ability of GEMONN in training CNNs, we consider the LeNet‐5 [52] and its variant (termed LeNet‐deeper) having more convolutional operations and more filters, as shown in Fig. 9.6(c), where a ReLu [53] activation function follows each convolutional operation. To investigate the results on deeper CNNs, a Vgg16 [54] variant with channel setting [8, 16, 32, 55] is employed, whose last two FC layers are set to 512 and 256. Besides, an effective cell‐based CNN [56] is also considered, termed Cell‐CNN, whose normal cell and reduction cell are set to the best architecture founded in [18], as plotted in Fig. 9.6(b) and (d). To facilitate the training of the Cell‐CNN, as suggested in [24], the neural network contains 6 cells, 16 filters in all the nodes, and an auxiliary head classifier with a loss weight of 0.4.

9.2.4.2 Benchmark Datasets

As listed in Table 9.1, 17 widely used datasets are adopted in the experiments. The first 10 datasets including MNIST [52] as well as its variants [57] and Cifar10‐bw [58] are used in the experiments in training AE and SAE. The next six datasets are collected from the UCR time series classification archive [59] and used in the experiments of training LSTMs. Besides, the last dataset Cifar10 [58] is used in the experiments of CNNs.

9.2.4.3 Compared Algorithms

Since the experiments are conducted on AE, SAE, LSTM, and CNNs, different comparison approaches have to be selected for different NNs.

Algorithms for Training AE The following comparison approaches are chosen for training the AE:

  • SGD [4]. Stochastic GD;
  • Adam [6]. A method for stochastic optimization;
  • NSGA‐II [44]. NSGA‐II with SBX operator;
  • NSGA‐II (+gradient). Based on NSGA‐II, update all offspring solutions by SGD for one step at each generation;
  • NSGA‐II (+gradient). Based on NSGA‐II, update all offspring solutions by SSGD for one step at each generation;
  • GEMONN (SSGD). GEMONN without updating the Pareto optimal solutions by SSGD;
  • GEMONN (single). GEMONN without optimizing sparsity by Eq. (9.16);
  • GEMONN (S). GEMONN without considering sparsity by Eqs. (9.13) and (9.14);
  • GEMONN (G). GEMONN without using gradient information by Eqs. (9.8), (9.9), (9.11), and (9.12).

SGD and Adam are two most popular gradient‐based approaches for training DNNs with millions of weights, which can be used as baselines to validate whether the performance of GEMONN is promising or not. NSGA‐II, NSGA‐II (+gradient), and NSGA‐II (+gradient) are used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed genetic operator gSBX, since the other components of NSGA‐II and GEMONN, i.e., solution evaluation, mating selection, and environmental selection, are completely the same. The remaining GEMONN (SSGD), GEMONN(single), GEMONN (S), and GEMONN (G) are designed for ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN.

Approaches for Training SAE The following state‐of‐the‐art approaches are used for training SAE:

  • SDAE [60]. Stacked denoising AEs;
  • SCAE [61]. Stacked contractive AEs;
  • SSAE [62]. Stacked sparse AEs;
  • EUDNN [11]. An evolutionary approach for training unsupervised DNNs.

As introduced in [11], SDAE, SCAE, and SSAE are three state‐of‐the‐art gradient‐based approaches for training SAE, which incorporate various problem independent regularization terms to decrease the network complexity for alleviating overfitting. Besides, the evolutionary approach EUDNN is considered as the state‐of‐the‐art, which can effectively train large‐scale DNNs with the help of dimensionality reduction. As a result, the comparison between GEMONN and the chosen algorithms is meaningful and convincing.

Algorithms for Training LSTM and CNNs Only SGD and Adam are considered for training LSTM and CNNs in the comparative studies, since these two approaches are very popular and effective for optimizing the large number of weights together. Besides, existing EAs, including EUDNN, are not well suited for training them due to their poor performance resulted from the curse of dimensionality.

9.2.4.4 Parameter Settings

The parameter settings for all the compared approaches are given below.

Parameters in Training AE The number of hidden units of the AE is set to 500, which means that the total number of weights to be optimized is . Besides, the following settings are used in the compared approaches:

  • SGD and Adam. The learning rate varies in ; the batch size is set to 64; and the maximal number of training steps is set to , to be consistent with the evolutionary approaches.
  • NSGA‐II and its variants. The population size is set to 50; the maximum number of generations is set to 500.
  • GEMONN and its variants. The population size is set to 50 and the maximum generation is set to 500.

As a result, all the compared approaches have the same number of function evaluations that calculates the output and the gradient over all the training samples for fairness.

Parameters in training SAE The number of units in each layer of SAE is empirically set to [, 500, 400, 300, 200, 100, ], where is the dimension of features and is the number of classes of the dataset. The following parameter settings are used in the comparative studies, which also ensures that all the compared approaches consume the same number of function evaluations:

  • SDAE, SCAE, and SSAE. Following the settings in [11], the SGD is chosen as the training approach, where the learning rate varies in , and the batch size is set to 64; the maximum number of training epochs is set to ; the binary corrupted level of SDAE, the sparsity of SSAE, the coefficient of the contractive term in SCAE is set to , respectively.
  • EUDNN. The population size is set to 50; the maximum iteration is set to 500; other parameters follow the original settings in the literature.
  • GEMONN. The population size is set to 50; maximum generation is set to 500.

Parameters in Training LSTM and CNNs The sizes of the input layer, hidden layer, and output layer of a 2‐layer LSTM are set to , 100, and , respectively, and the parameters in CNNs are presented in Section 9.2.4.1. The following settings are used in the compared approaches:

  • SGD and Adam. The learning rate varies in , and the batch size is set to 64 for LSTM and CNNs; The maximum number of training epochs is set to for LSTM and for CNNs.
  • GEMONN. The population size is set to 50; and the maximum number of generations is set to 100 for LSTM and 500 for CNNs.

All models and the gradient‐based approaches are implemented in Pytorch [63], and GEMONN as well as variants of NSGA‐II are implemented in Numpy [64]. These experiments were performed on a Windows 10 computer with an Intel i7‐8700k CPU and an NVIDIA 1080 GPU. The source code of the proposed approach is made available from https://github.com/smartdonckey/GEMONN.

9.2.4.5 Experimental Results on AE

Figure 9.7 presents the solutions obtained by all algorithms under comparison in the objective space. It can also be found that the performance of SGD and Adam highly relies on the learning rate, as the solutions obtained by SGD (0.1) outperform SGD (0.01) and SGD (0.001), while Adam (0.1) is also much worse than Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001). Moreover, the solutions obtained by SGD and Adam are not sparse at all, which may affect the generalization of the model and result in overfitting.

On the other hand, the solutions obtained by NSGA‐II have poor convergence in terms of the MSE and we cannot find any valuable solution due to the poor search ability of the existing genetic operators. With the assistance of the gradient information, the solutions obtained by NSGA‐II (+gradient) are better than those obtained by NSGA‐II, which verifies the importance of introducing gradient information into EAs. Nevertheless, the performance of NSGA‐II and its variants is much worse than the gradient‐based approaches and the proposed GEMONN.

The proposed GEMONN exhibits quite competitive performance compared to SGD, Adam, and NSGA‐II. On the one hand, it can be seen that the solutions acquired by GEMONN are very promising, whose MSE is just worse than those obtained by Adam (0.001) and Adam (0.01) but much better than those obtained by the other approaches. On the other hand, the sparsity of the solutions acquired by GEMONN is similar to those obtained by NSGA‐II but much better than those obtained by SGD and Adam. In short, the AE trained by the proposed GEMONN can have a relatively low MSE with satisfactory sparsity.

To investigate the convergence speed of the compared approaches, Fig. 9.8 depicts the decline in MSE of all the compared approaches, with the increase of the number of function evaluations, where the observation is consistent with Fig. 9.7. More specifically, GEMONN outperforms NSGA‐II and most gradient‐based approaches, while it converges slower than Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001).

As a result, solutions obtained by the proposed GEMONN have better sparsity but worse training loss than those obtained by Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001). To further investigate which solutions are better for classification, an FC layer is tailored for the AE and trained in a supervised manner. Figure 9.9 presents the mean correct classification rate (CCR) [11] on test set obtained by SGD, Adam, and the proposed GEMONN, averaged over 30 runs. Besides, a three‐layer FC network with the same size is directly trained for the classification task and used as the baseline. By contrast, the results of NSGA‐II are ignored since the obtained CCR values are quite poor. It can be observed from Fig. 9.9 that the mean CCR values obtained by GEMONN are better than all the other compared approaches including Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001), though the solutions found by Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001) are with lower MSE than GEMONN as shown in Fig. 9.8. Therefore, it can be inferred that the AEs trained by Adam overfit the training set to some extent, whereas the sparse AEs obtained by GEMONN can alleviate overfitting.

For visual observation of the difference between the sparsity of the AEs obtained by the compared approaches, Fig. 9.10 draws the connections between the input layer and hidden layer of the AEs obtained by Adam (0.01), Adam (0.001), SGD (0.1), and GEMONN on the MNIST dataset, where a darker color indicates a denser connection between weights. It is obvious that the AE obtained by GEMONN is much sparser than those obtained by the gradient‐based approaches. Moreover, Fig. 9.11 plots the connections between the input layer and the hidden layer of the AE obtained by GEMONN at different generations on the MNIST dataset. For better visualization, each graphic in Fig. 9.11 consists of 500 binary images, where each image has pixels and each pixel indicates whether the corresponding input unit is connected to a hidden unit or not. Besides, a gray pixel indicates a connection between the input unit and a hidden unit, while a white dot indicates there is no connection. As can be seen from Fig. 9.11, the AE is not sparse at the beginning, while it gradually becomes sparse as the population evolves. As a consequence, the proposed GEMONN can effectively control the sparsity of the obtained NN, and such a sparse nature is crucial for preventing the model from overfitting.

Afterward, the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN is verified by ablation studies. First, GEMONN is compared to GEMONN (SSGD) on the MNIST dataset to verify the effectiveness of the SSGD based the update strategy for Pareto optimal solutions. According to the solutions obtained by GEMONN and GEMONN (SSGD) shown in Fig. 9.12(a), it is clear that the solutions obtained by GEMONN dominate most solutions obtained by GEMONN (SSGD), hence the effectiveness of SSGD is confirmed. Second, Fig. 9.12(b) depicts the effectiveness of considering the optimization of sparsity within GEMONN. As can be seen that the final solutions of GEMONN (single) have higher training CCR values than that of GEMONN on all 10 datasets, however, GEMONN can obtain better test CCR values than GEMONN (single). The crucial reason is that GEMONN (single) encounters the overfitting problem to some extent due to the optimization not considering the sparsity restriction. According to the above comparisons in Figs. 9.8, 9.9, and 9.12(b), it is indeed an effective way to mitigate the overfitting by considering sparsity in optimization. Third, GEMONN is compared to GEMONN (G) and GEMONN (S) on the MNIST dataset to verify the effectiveness of the gradient information in the proposed genetic operator. As can be seen from Fig. 9.13(a), the solutions obtained by GEMONN are superior over those obtained by GEMONN (G) and GEMONN (S) in terms of both the sparsity and MSE. Besides, GEMONN converges significantly faster than GEMONN (G) and GEMONN (S) in terms of the hypervolume indicator (HV) [55], as shown in Fig. 9.13(b). Therefore, the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN can be verified.

Lastly, a parameter sensitivity analysis of the population size and distribution index in GEMONN is conducted. Figure 9.14(a) shows the HV values obtained by GEMONN on four datasets MNIST, MNIST‐rot, rectangles, and convex with different population sizes, where it can be seen that GEMONN can obtain a relatively good performance when the population size is larger than 50. It is not necessary to set to 100 for a slightly higher HV value at the expense of a doubled number of fitness evaluations. The results of sensitivity analysis of the distribution index in GEMONN on four datasets TwoPatterns, ECG5000, UWaveGestureLibraryX, and InsectWingbeatSound are plotted in Fig. 9.14(b). From this figure, we can see that the proposed GEMONN can obtain the best performance with the distribution index being equal to 15 or 20. Thus, the recommended in [35] is also suitable and effective for GEMONN.

9.2.4.6 Experimental Results on SAE

Table 9.2 lists the CCR values of the SAEs obtained by GEMONN, EUDNN, SSAE, SCAE, and SDAE on the nine Datasets, where each cell in the table records the mean and standard deviation of the CCR values obtained in 30 independent runs. In addition, the Wilcoxon rank sum test [65] at a significance level of 0.05 is employed to perform statistical analysis on the experimental results, where the symbols “,” “,” and “” indicate that the result obtained by GEMONN is significantly better than, significantly worse than, and statistically similar to that of the corresponding peer competitors, respectively.

It is clearly presented in Table 9.2 that the proposed GEMONN acquires the best results on seven out of nine datasets, which is followed by EUDNN and SSAE obtaining one best result. In terms of the Wilcoxon rank sum test, the number of datasets where GEMONN performs statistically better than EUDNN, SSAE, SCAE, and SDAE are 6, 7, 8, and 9, respectively. Furthermore, Fig. 9.15 plots the connections between the layers of the SAEs obtained by SDAE, SCAE, SSAE, EUDNN, and GEMONN on the Cifar10‐bw dataset. Clearly, the SAE obtained by GEMONN is much sparser than those obtained by the other approaches. Therefore, it can be concluded that the SAE obtained by GEMONN has not only better classification performance but also much lower complexity than those obtained by the other compared approaches. In short, the proposed GEMONN shows significant superiority over the state‐of‐the‐art approaches in training SAE.

Next, Table 9.3 lists the runtimes of the proposed GEMONN, EUDNN, and three approaches trained by SGD on the ten datasets. It can be found that the efficiency of EUDNN is the worst due to its expensive evaluations, and the efficiency of GEMONN is better than EUDNN but worse than SGD, though it has the same time complexity to SGD as analyzed in Section 9.2.3.4. This is mainly because SGD is implemented by Pytorch on GPU, while the proposed GEMONN is implemented on CPU since some complex steps in EA cannot be easily performed on GPU, which is a common difficulty of most EA‐based approaches including EUDNN.

9.2.4.7 Experimental Results on LSTM and CNNs

The comparison between the proposed GEMONN and gradient‐based approaches in training LSTM is presented in Table 9.4. The results are calculated based on 30 independent runs, and the Wilcoxon rank sum test is also employed. Note that due to the poor performance of Adam (0.1) and SGD (0.001), only the results of Adam (0.001), Adam (0.01), SGD (0.01), and SGD (0.1) are listed in the table. As can be seen, the overall performance of GEMONN is better than the gradient‐based approaches, having achieved the largest average CCR values on four out of six datasets. Besides, Adam (0.01) and SGD (0.1) obtain the largest average CCR values on the remaining two datasets. In short, the performance of GEMONN is significantly better than Adam (0.001) as well as SGD (0.01) and competitive to Adam (0.01) and SGD (0.1). In addition, it is worth to note that the performance of Adam is sensitive to the learning rate since Adam (0.01) outperforms Adam (0.001) on ECG5000 and ElectricDevicess, but Adam (0.001) outperforms Adam (0.01) on FordA and UWaveGestureLibraryX. By contrast, the GEMONN does not contain the learning rate or any other sensitive parameter, which is also a superiority of evolutionary approaches over gradient‐based approaches.

The comparative results between GEMONN and the gradient‐based approaches in training CNNs on Cifar10 dataset are shown in Fig. 9.16, where the mean test accuracy over 30 independent runs is plotted. Note that the result of SGD (0.001) is not given due to its poor performance. From this figure, it can be observed that GEMONN outperforms gradient‐based approaches on LeNet‐5, and the performance of GEMONN is also slightly better than the opponents on LeNet‐deeper. However, Adam (0.001) and Adam (0.01) get the best performance on Vgg16‐variant as well as Cell‐CNN, while GEMONN obtains a competitive performance. It is worth noting that the performance of GEMONN degenerates with the architecture of CNN becoming complex since the proportion of convolutional operation parameters increases from 5% to 98%. Essentially, the weights of a whole CNN can be divided into two parts, including the feature extraction (convolutional) part and the classifier (FC) part. Compared to weights of the FC layers, convolutional operations have much fewer weights due to the intrinsic merit of local connection and weight‐sharing, where most weights of convolutional layers should not be optimized to zero during the training process [66]. To gain a deep insight into the weights of each part obtained by GEMONN, Fig. 9.17 depicts the percentage of nonzero weights in four CNNs obtained by GEMONN and Adam. It is clear that the weights of convolutional layers obtained by the proposed approach are much sparser than that of Adam; hence, the final performance of GEMONN may be slightly worse than the best gradient‐based approaches. Nevertheless, EMONN still holds a competitive performance compared to SGD and Adam.

9.3 Action Command Encoding‐Based Surrogate‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm for Neural Architecture Search

NAS appeared in the 1980s [67] and manifested an explosive growth in recent years [23], where various optimizers have been adopted to automatically determine the desired hyperparameters and topologies of neural networks especially CNNs. For example, NEAT [29] optimizes both the topologies and weights of feedforward neural networks by genetic algorithm; The work in [68] adopts the tree‐structured Parzen estimator (TPE) [69] to optimize the hyperparameters of CNNs, which represents the search space as an expression graph and optimizes the loss function by sampling hyperparameters in the graph; NAS [17] uses a controller recurrent neural network to generate the hyperparameters and topologies of CNNs and trains the controller by a policy gradient method [70]; NAO [21] embeds the hyperparameters and topologies of CNNs into a continuous space by using an LSTM [50], then optimizes it through GD. As can be seen, there have been many optimizers adopted in NAS, such as EAs (e.g., NEAT), Bayesian optimization (e.g., TPE), RL (e.g., NAS), and GD (e.g., NAO). However, only a few encoding schemes have been designed to provide an effective search space to be explored by these optimizers. In addition, although these search methods can generate better architectures than hand‐crafted ones, the performance is improved at the expense of computational resources, where many search methods are criticized for the high computational cost of the search process or the large complexity of the found architectures. In this section, we would like to take a step forward along this line of research, aiming to improve the performance of NAS by presenting a novel encoding scheme, and we also would like to propose an effective EA for NAS with the assistance of the encoding scheme due to the various merits of EAs. However, since EAs are population‐based optimizers, it will further aggravate the expensive computational cost in NAS.

To this end, this section introduces an action command encoding‐based surrogate assisted EA, termed ACEncoding, for NAS by designing a novel encoding scheme and an effective surrogate model. In the proposed action command encoding scheme, an architecture is constructed by some action commands and each action command is specified by three adjoined integers. By predefining a series of action commands including adding a layer, adding a connection, and cloning a local module, the proposed encoding scheme can use multiple action commands to construct complex architectures in a generative manner. Considering that architectures are represented by a variable‐length sequence of integers within a finite range, thus the surrogate model, called Seq2Rank, converts the sequence to a fixed‐length vector by a Seq2Seq model [71], then uses a RankNet [72] to predict the rankings of architectures.

In the following, we first present the mathematical formulation of NAS, then the action command encoding method, the performance evaluator‐based surrogate model, and the framework of the proposed ACEncoding are subsequently presented. Finally, experimental comparisons between the ACEncoding and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for searching CNNs are presented and discussed.

9.3.1 Problem Formulation of Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search

Given a data set , the NAS can be formulated as the following single‐objective optimization problem.

Due to the enormous demand for small‐sized networks in real‐world applications, the model complexity is also considered in the NAS task [24], and thus NAS can be formulated as a bi‐objective optimization problem as follows:

where is the classification error rate of on validation dataset and denotes the model complexity of . The model complexity can be measured by the number of model parameters, the number of floating‐point operations, and inference time [24]. In this chapter, we adopt the bi‐objective optimization problem formulation for NAS, where the number of model parameters is used to measure the model complexity.

9.3.2 Action Command Encoding Scheme

9.3.2.1 Action Commands in the Encoding Scheme

The proposed action command encoding scheme is inspired by the process of gene expression, where each architecture is constructed by a series of action commands and each action command is encoded by three integers. Regarding an architecture as a directed acyclic graph , the action command encoding scheme does not directly encode the layer set or connection set like existing encoding schemes; instead, the architecture grows from empty according to the action commands in the encoding. In the encoding scheme, the following two basic action commands are defined:

  1. (1) Adding a new layer to the architecture.

  2. (2) Adding a new connection to the architecture.

    Obviously, these two action commands are enough to represent arbitrary topologies, which is the same as the graph‐based encoding.

    However, the encoding will be very long when representing large architectures with dense connections; hence, the following two action commands are also considered in the encoding scheme:

  3. (3) Adding a new layer in parallel with an existing one, i.e., the two layers have the same predecessors and successors.
  4. (4) Adding a new layer after an existing one, i.e., the successors of the new layer are set to the same as the existing layer, then the successor of the existing layer is set to the new layer.

These two action commands can generate some complex topologies like the widely used block‐based topology consisting of two parallel layers [56]; hence, we believe that they are helpful to find desired architectures more efficiently. Note that the combination operation is omitted here, which is fixed to the element‐wise addition as suggested in many existing encoding schemes [21, 73, 74]. It is obvious that the graph‐based encoding should use many operations (i.e., adding a new layer and adding multiple connections) to achieve each of these two action commands, especially when the existing layer is connected to many other layers.

Moreover, it has been well recognized that many successful architectures, including GoogLeNet, ResNet, and those generated by block‐based encoding, are composed of repeated modules [75]. Therefore, the following two action commands are designed to repeat the local modules in the architecture:

  1. (5) Cloning an existing local module and locating the two local modules in parallel, i.e., the two modules have the same predecessors and successors.
  2. (6) Cloning an existing local module and locating the two local modules in sequence, i.e., the successors of the new module are set to the same as the existing module, then the successor of the existing module is set to the new module.

Here, a local module is defined as a set of layers connected in a chain‐like structure with no branching. Besides, another action command is designed to represent the dense block like those in DenseNet:

  1. (7) Making an existing local module a densely connected block, i.e., each layer is connected to all the others in the module.

By using these seven action commands, the proposed encoding scheme can represent arbitrary topologies and encode some popular blocks in a short sequence. Since these action commands are designed according to the topologies of some popular architectures, the proposed encoding scheme is free to be extended by more action commands for representing the topologies of other effective architectures. Note that each action command does not necessarily appear in the encoding, as an action command will be weeded out during the search process if it always brings a bad performance to the architecture. Besides, it is noteworthy that some basic action commands (e.g., adding a layer or connection) have been adopted in the mutation operator of EA‐based search methods [22, 76], but these action commands cannot be achieved by other optimizers. By contrast, the encoding scheme encodes these action commands in a sequence that can be explored by different optimizers, where an EA, RL, and GD are employed in the experiments.

9.3.2.2 Decoding Process of the Proposed Action Command Encoding Scheme

Table 9.5 lists the codon of each action command, where each action command is represented by three integers with different meanings. The first integer in each codon varies from 1 to 7 denoting the index of an action command, while the second and third integers can be one of the three variables , , and . denotes the type of layer to be added, which varies from 1 to 10 denoting one of the following 10 operations as suggested in [21]: (1) convolution; (2) convolution; (3) convolution; (4) convolution; (5) max pooling; (6) max pooling; (7) max pooling; (8) average pooling; (9) average pooling; (10) average pooling. Note that all the operations are tailed by batch normalization. denotes the index of an existing layer; note that the first two indices denote the input layer and output layer rather than the generated convolutional or pooling layers. denotes the length of a local module with chain‐like structure, which consists of layers starting from an existing layer.

Figure 9.18 depicts an example to illustrate the decoding process of the encoding scheme, where the sequence contains six action commands determined by 18 integers. The initial architecture has two inputs and an output, and it grows according to the following action commands to form an architecture having 9 layers and 12 connections: Adding a convolutional layer, adding a pooling layer, adding a connection, adding a pooling layer, adding a convolutional layer, and cloning a module. It is worth noting that the action commands do not specify the successor when adding a layer, where the successor is set to the output layer by default (e.g., the connection between the convolutional layer and the output layer shown in Fig. 9.18(a)). If this layer is specified as the predecessor of other layers by the subsequent action commands, the default connection between this layer and the output layer is omitted.

In order to provide a finite search space, the variables and in the codon are restricted to be less than a maximum value. This maximum value is set to 30 in the experiments, which is enough to represent a relatively large architecture. In addition, since some large values of or may lead to invalid action commands, they are revised by specific strategies in the decoding process. First, if the layer index is larger than the number of existing layers , is changed to . Second, if the module length exceeds the maximum length of the module (i.e., reaching the output layer or a layer having multiple branches), is changed to the maximum length of the module. Third, if the architecture becomes cyclic after adding a connection, the connection is reversed. The procedure of the decoding process of ACEnoding is summarized in Algorithm 9.3.

9.3.2.3 Remarks

It can be found from Fig. 9.18 that the proposed action command encoding scheme constructs an architecture with a relatively complex topology by using 18 variables. On the contrary, the adjacent matrix‐based encoding requires variables to represent the same topology, the graph‐based encoding requires 6 variables to store the layers and variables to store the connections, and the block‐based encoding needs to use four blocks determined by variables to represent a similar architecture with fewer connections. The shorter encoding is owing to the delicate action commands that inherit the advantages of both graph‐based encoding and block‐based encoding, which provide a more compact search space that facilitates the optimization of architectures. The trade‐off between the length of encoding and the complexity of the represented architecture is automatically balanced by optimizers in the search process, where a bias toward the first four action commands in Table 9.5 leads to more complex architectures and a bias toward the last three action commands makes the encoding shorter. The main difference between the proposed action command encoding scheme and existing encoding schemes are summarized in the following.

  • Action command encoding scheme vs. hyperparameter‐based encoding and adjacent matrix‐based encoding. The hyperparameter‐based encoding and adjacent matrix‐based encoding can only represent the hyperparameters and topologies of architectures, respectively, while the proposed action command encoding scheme can represent both of them. Besides, the proposed encoding scheme specifies a topology by using a series of action commands stored in a sequence, which is much shorter than the adjacent matrix.
  • Action command encoding scheme vs. graph‐based encoding. The proposed action command encoding scheme is equivalent to the graph‐based encoding when using only the first two action commands, which are enough to represent arbitrary topologies. By contrast, the proposed encoding scheme can represent specific complex topologies by the other action commands, which cannot be represented by the graph‐based encoding using a short sequence.
  • Action command encoding scheme vs. block‐based encoding. Both the proposed action command encoding scheme and the block‐based encoding can represent complex topologies using a short encoding. However, the topologies that can be represented by block‐based encoding are limited by the topology of a single block, whereas arbitrary topologies can be represented by the proposed encoding scheme.

9.3.3 Performance Evaluator‐Based Surrogate Model

9.3.3.1 Architecture Embedding

The general architecture of Seq2Rank is illustrated in Fig. 9.19. As can be seen, the model for architecture embedding consists of a FC layer for word embedding and an LSTM layer used in the Seq2Seq model. To begin with, an architecture represented by the proposed action command encoding scheme is tokenized by regarding the codon of each action command as a token; besides, an <SOS> token and an <EOS> token are attached to the start and end of each sequence, respectively, and an <MOS> token is also required to split the action commands for normal cell and reduction cell if the cell structure is adopted. Then, each token is converted to one‐hot representation and fed to the embedding layer to obtain a word vector. Afterward, a Seq2Seq model is trained by maximizing the following conditional probability:

where is an input sequence, is the target output sequence, and is the hidden states of the input sequence. The conditional probability depends on all the hidden states rather than the last one since the attention mechanism is adopted.

To convert the variable‐length sequence of the proposed action command encoding to a fixed‐length sequence, a large number of training samples should be generated to train the above model in an unsupervised manner. That is, the input sequence and target output sequence of each sample are the same architecture represented by the proposed encoding scheme. Therefore, we randomly generate three million architectures beforehand to train the model until convergence. 9.3.3.2 Performance Prediction

The performance of each architecture is estimated by predicting its ranking among multiple architectures via RankNet. The RankNet adopted here is a feedforward neural network with two hidden layers, where the input includes the fixed‐length sequences of two architectures and the output indicates which one of the two architectures has a better performance. Then, the RankNet can be trained by minimizing the following cross‐entropy cost function:

(9.23)

where is the target label.

In contrast to the Seq2Seq model that can be trained in advance, the RankNet should be trained during the search process in a supervised manner, as the target label has to be obtained by comparing the validation accuracies of two architectures. Given the fixed‐length sequences of architectures and their validation accuracies , the training set for RankNet is formed as , where and there are training samples in total. In practice, a number of architectures should be evaluated via training and validation at the beginning of the search process, then they are used to train the RankNet. During the search process, the performance of most candidate architectures is evaluated via RankNet, while some promising ones can be evaluated via training and validation and used to update the RankNet to enhance its ranking accuracy in the desired search regions.

9.3.4 Framework of ACEncoding

To simultaneously optimize the accuracy and complexity of neural architecture in NAS, the proposed ACEncoding employs NSGA‐II as the optimizer due to its high competitiveness in solving bi‐objective optimization problems [77]. Compared with existing work on NSGA‐II for NAS, the proposed ACEncoding is characterized with two key aspects: an effective action command encoding scheme for NAS, and an efficient performance evaluator‐based strategy for accelerating the search. Specifically, Algorithm 9.4 presents the main steps of the proposed ACEncoding with the surrogate model Seq2Rank under NSGA‐II, which mainly consists of seven steps.

First, train a Seq2Seq model based on an amount of sequential data in advance. Second, randomly generate a population consisting of solutions which represent corresponding neural architectures, and decode and evaluate the solutions in after training their corresponding architectures to compute their objective values in Eq. (9.3.1). Then, the surrogate model, i.e., the Seq2Rank performance evaluator, is initially trained with the initial population's information (including all architecture' encoding and performance) based on the pretrained Seq2Seq model. Fourth, the binary tournament selection [24] is applied to the population to mate individuals in the population and generate the parent population . Fifth, an offspring population is produced from the parent population by implementing the crossover and mutation operators proposed in NSGA‐Net [24]. Sixth, determine whether the solutions in at the current generation need to train their architecture for evaluation: if yes, decode and evaluate the solutions in after training their corresponding architectures to compute their objective values in Eq. (9.3.1); otherwise, directly obtain the architecture performance of all solutions in by the surrogate model Seq2Rank. Finally, the main population and the offspring population will be concatenated together, and the standard environmental selection operation in NSGA‐II [44] is used to select better solutions as the new main population . The second to the seventh step will repeat until the evolution termination criteria is satisfied, after which the non‐dominated individuals will be output.

9.3.5 Experimental Studies

9.3.5.1 Performance Verification of Action Command Encoding

Actually, the action command encoding scheme devised in the proposed ACEncoding can be used for any other optimizers, including RL and gradient optimization. To validate the effectiveness of the devised action command encoding scheme in encoding, we compared the devised encoding scheme with NSGA‐Net, MetaQNN [82] and NAO [21], where NSGA‐Net is based on an EA and the adjacent matrix‐based encoding, MetaQNN is based on RL and the hyperparameter‐based encoding, and NAO is based on GD and the block‐based encoding. Hence, it is reasonable to adopt these three methods to compare the proposed action command encoding scheme with other encoding schemes on different optimizers. The parameter settings mainly follow those in the original papers of the three methods, the details of which are given in the following.

  • Structure of CNN. The widely used cell structure is adopted in ACEncoding to decrease the search space. Specifically, a normal cell and a reduction cell are encoded by the proposed encoding scheme independently, and the whole CNN consists of three normal cells and two reduction cells stacked alternately. For the hyperparameters in the convolutional and pooling layers, the filter size is determined by the encoding, the number of filters is always set to 16, and the stride size is set to 2 for the layers directly connected to the reduction cell's inputs and 1 for all the other layers.
  • ACEncoding and NSGA‐Net. The only difference between NSGA‐Net and NSGA‐Net is the adopted encoding scheme, where NSGA‐Net adopts the adjacent matrix‐based encoding. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, the optimizer randomly initializes a population with 40 architectures having 10–20 action commands for each cell, and then evolves the population for 25 generations to generate 1000 architectures in total. Since the crossover and mutation operators in NSGA‐Net are tailored for the binary adjacent matrix, new crossover and mutation operators are designed for the proposed action command encoding scheme. To be specific, the crossover operator randomly selects an anchor point from the encodings of two parent architectures and exchanges the action commands after the anchor point of the two encodings to generate two offspring architectures. The offspring architectures are then mutated by one of the three operations, including adding a random action command, randomly deleting an action command, and randomly changing the variables of an action command. The crossover probability is 1 and the mutation probability is 0.1.
  • ACEncoding with RL as the optimizer, termed ACEncoding under RL. MetaQNN iteratively generates architectures according to a ‐table and updates the ‐table according to the performance of the generated architectures via ‐learning. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, each action command is regarded as a state and the ‐table stores the value denoting the reward of selecting action command after action command . To generate an architecture, the agent sequentially selects action commands via the ‐greedy strategy according to the ‐table, until the termination state is selected or 20 action commands have been selected. This procedure repeats twice to generate the normal cell and reduction cell of an architecture, and the generated architecture is evaluated and stored in a replay dictionary for periodically updating the ‐values between action commands in the ‐table. The ‐learning rate is set to 0.1, the discount factor is set to 1 (i.e., there are no over‐prioritize short‐term rewards), and the parameter is set to 1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 when 200, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 850, 900, 950, and 1000 architectures have been evaluated.
  • ACEncoding with GD as the optimizer, termed ACEncoding under GD. NAO adopts an encoder LSTM to embed the architecture into a continuous space and takes the continuous representation as input to predict its performance by a feedforward neural network. Thus, better continuous representation can be obtained by moving the input along the gradient direction induced by the performance, and the updated continuous representation is fed into a decoder LSTM to generate a new architecture. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, the optimizer randomly initializes 600 architectures having 20 action commands for each cell, as the length of the decoder is fixed in NAO. Then, these architectures are evaluated and used to train the two LSTMs and the feedforward neural network jointly. Afterward, 200 new architectures are generated by performing GD on the best 200 architectures. The last step repeats twice to form 1000 architectures generated in total. The sizes of the embedding layer, the hidden layer of the LSTMs, and the hidden layer of the feedforward neural network are set to 64, 128, and 200, respectively, and the models are trained using Adam [6] for 1000 epochs with a learning rate of 0.001.
  • Performance evaluation strategy. All the above three methods generate 1000 architectures during the whole search process. Each architecture is evaluated via training and validation without using parameter sharing or surrogate model, where the 50,000 images in CIFAR‐10 are randomly split into a training set of 45,000 samples and a validation set of 5000 samples. Each architecture is trained by SGD with a batch size of 128, a momentum of 0.9, and a learning rate ranging from 0.1 to 0.001 following a single‐period cosine schedule. The training samples are normalized and randomly augmented by several data pre‐processing techniques, including random crop (i.e., padding each image by 4 pixels and cropping a random patch), horizontal flipping [13], and cutout (with a mask length of 16) [84]. Besides, the scheduled path dropout (with a probability of 0.2) [56] and an auxiliary classifier (appended to the architecture at 2/3 depth with a constant factor of 0.4) [16] are adopted in the training process.

Figure 9.20 plots the minimum validation error during the search process of the original NSGA‐Net, MetaQNN, and NAO and those integrated with the proposed action command encoding scheme, where NSGA‐Net with the devised encoding scheme is actually ACEncoding. It can be found that the proposed action command encoding scheme is competitive to the adjacent matrix‐based encoding on NSGA‐Net, while the devised encoding scheme converges obviously faster than the hyperparameter‐based encoding on MetaQNN and the block‐based encoding on NAO. Therefore, it can be concluded that the proposed action command encoding scheme is suitable for different optimizers including EAs, RL, and GD, and it is competitive to or more effective than existing encoding schemes.

9.3.5.2 Performance Comparison on CIFAR‐10

Table 9.6 presents the test error of 31 CNNs found by human experts and 17 NAS methods. It can be observed that the CNNs obtained by ACEncoding have 2.80% to 3.16% test errors and 2.4M to 3.2M parameters, which are quite competitive with the other CNNs listed in the table. As for ACEncoding, the test error of the obtained CNN is slightly higher than the CNN obtained by ACEncoding without Seq2Rank; by contrast, the search cost can decrease to 1.5 GPU days from 7 GPU days. Furthermore, the CNN obtained by the proposed ACEncoding is enlarged by setting the number of filters to 96, denoted as ACEncoding (more filters), which can lead to a test error of 2.32%, better than all the other CNNs in the table.

Figure 9.21 depicts the test error and number of parameters of the CNNs listed in Table 9.6. It can be found that there are four CNNs having the best trade‐offs between test error and complexity, where two of them are obtained by the proposed ACEncoding, one of them is obtained by NASNet, and the remaining one is wide ResNet. It should be noted that NASNet obtains the CNN by searching for 2000 GPU days, whereas the proposed ACEncoding consumes only 1.5 GPU days. Although the wide ResNet is manually designed with no search cost, its test error is much higher than the other three CNNs. Besides, Fig. 9.22 plots the test error and search cost of the CNNs, where the best trade‐off CNN found by the proposed ACEncoding has larger search cost but lower test error than the other trade‐off CNNs. In short, the proposed ACEncoding can strike a balance among the search performance, the complexity of architectures, and the computational cost of search process.

For a visual observation, Fig. 9.23 depicts the architectures of the normal cell and reduction cell found by the proposed ACEncoding. It can be seen that the architectures have more than 10 layers with many connections. For adjacent matrix‐based encoding and graph‐based encoding, they require a long sequence of variables to represent such complex architectures. Besides, the block‐based encoding is almost impossible to represent these architectures by the block‐based topology.

9.3.5.3 Performance Comparison on CIFAR‐100

The transferability of the architectures found by the proposed ACEncoding and its variants is then verified on CIFAR‐100 [58], where the same CNNs are trained by the 50,000 training samples of CIFAR‐100 and tested on the 10,000 test samples. According to the results listed in Table 9.7, the CNNs obtained by the proposed ACEncoding and its variants also have competitive test errors and complexities to the others. Besides, the CNN generated based on the second best architecture found by the proposed ACEncoding is evaluated, which has higher complexity but lower test error than the other CNNs obtained by its variants.

Figure 9.24 depicts the test error and number of parameters of the CNNs listed in Table 9.6. Obviously, the proposed ACEncoding can also obtain two trade‐off CNNs, and NAO can obtain one trade‐off CNN. Although the CNN obtained by NAO has the lowest test error, it is found by searching for 200 GPU days, which is much higher than the 1.5 GPU days consumed by the proposed ACEncoding. As can be further observed from Fig. 9.25, the CNN found by the proposed ACEncoding strikes good balance between test error and search cost. In short, the architectures found by the proposed ACEncoding are transferable to more complex datasets.

9.3.5.4 Performance Comparison on Fashion‐MNIST

Lastly, Table 9.8 shows the test error and number of parameters of the architectures found by human experts and NAS methods on Fashion‐MNIST, which is an image classification dataset containing 60,000 training samples and 10,000 test samples [87]. It is obvious that the test error of the CNN obtained by the proposed ACEncoding is lower than all the other CNNs besides the one found by NAONet. Besides, the CNN found by NAONet has a significantly larger complexity than the CNN found by the proposed method. The experimental results further demonstrate that the proposed ACEncoding can hold a good balance between the performance and complexity of architectures.

9.3.5.5 Performance Verification of Seq2Rank

The proposed performance evaluator Seq2Rank is compared to two existing surrogate models for predicting the performance of architectures, namely, E2EPP [88] and Peephole [89]. E2EPP is an end‐to‐end performance predictor based on random forest [90], which is effective to a limited number of training samples and can directly handle the discrete variables without embedding. Peephole holds a similar pipeline to the proposed Seq2Rank, which embeds the architecture by an LSTM with embedding layer and predicts the performance by a feedforward neural network. However, Peephole concatenates all the hidden states but not using mean pooling or attention mechanism, and it predicts the validation accuracy rather than the ranking of each architecture. More importantly, Seq2Rank uses the Seq2Seq model to learn a continuous representation in an unsupervised manner, while Peephole directly trains the whole model in a supervised manner. For the models in Peephole and Seq2Rank, the sizes of the embedding layer, the hidden layer of the LSTM, and the two hidden layers of the feedforward neural network are set to 62, 120, 60, and 30, respectively, and the models are trained using SGD for 25 epochs with a learning rate of 0.1.

A number of 10,000 architectures represented by the devised action command encoding are randomly generated to form the dataset, where different numbers of samples are used as training samples and the rest are used as test samples. Table 9.9 lists the performance of E2EPP, Peephole, and Seq2Rank in terms of the Kendall's Tau metric, which is calculated by [91]

(9.24)

where is the total number of test samples and is the concordant pair that the predicted ranking is correct. Obviously, the value of Kendall's Tau ranges from 1 to 1 and a higher value corresponds to a higher accuracy. It can be found from the table that Peephole always has a worse performance than Seq2Rank, and E2EPP outperforms Seq2Rank only with 1000 training samples due to the superiority of random forest on small training sets. To summarize, it can be verified that Seq2Rank is more suitable for predicting the performance of architectures represented by the devised encoding than some existing surrogate‐assisted performance evaluators.

9.4 Summary

This chapter presents a gradient guide multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (GEMONN) and an action command encoding‐based surrogate‐assisted EA (ACEncoding) for the training of DNNs and NAS, respectively. Specifically, the proposed GEMONN focuses on designing a powerful genetic operator gSBX to directly optimize the weights of DNNs, by means of taking advantage of the gradient information. Moreover, the network sparsity is also optimized together with the training loss, which can reduce the network complexity and alleviate overfitting. Experimental results on single‐layer NNs, deep‐layer NNs, recurrent NNs, and CNNs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GEMONN. In short, this work not only introduces a novel approach for training deep NNs but also enhances the performance of EAs in solving large‐scale optimization problems.

For the proposed ACEncoding, a novel encoding scheme and a performance evaluator are presented for NAS. The proposed encoding scheme defines a set of action commands and encodes each architecture in a sequence consisting of the codons of multiple action commands. The proposed encoding scheme inherits the advantages of existing encoding schemes that can represent complex architectures as a relatively short sequence and has shown better effectiveness than some popular encoding schemes in EAs, RL, and GD. The proposed performance evaluator Seq2Rank adopts a Seq2Seq model to convert the variable‐length encoding of the action command into a fixed‐length sequence and then predicts the ranking of the architecture determined by the encoding via RankNet. The proposed performance evaluator has been empirically verified to be better than some existing surrogate models in predicting the performance of architectures represented by the proposed ACEncoding.
